strategy_title: Develop a rigorous framework for measuring AI agent reliability
strategy_text: Investigate how autonomous and semi-autonomous AI agents can be measured objectively, reproducibly, and meaningfully across diverse tasks and operating conditions. Build an evaluation framework that distinguishes superficial task completion from correctness, robustness, and dependable behavior. Audit representative agent benchmarks for task-selection effects, environmental variability, evaluator bias, contamination, and weak completion oracles. Define operational measures for end-to-end success, partial completion, error severity, recovery, repeat-trial consistency, tool-use correctness, and resources per successful outcome. Specify how to evaluate stochastic agents, long dependency chains, long-running tasks, external tools, and changing environments. Propose repeated-trial protocols, uncertainty intervals, failure-distribution reporting, and comparisons under controlled compute, time, tool, and monetary budgets. State the evidence and replication needed for defensible reliability claims; separate benchmark-specific gains from general improvements. Deliver a protocol with task strata, outcome rubrics, baseline comparisons, statistical analysis, and explicit limits on what its results can establish.

strategy_runs.strategy_title: Understand failure propagation and recovery in autonomous AI agents
strategy_runs.strategy_text: Map how agents fail during extended, multi-step tasks and determine which failures are detectable, recoverable, or silently corrupt later results. Examine incorrect reasoning and plans, tool misuse, incomplete observations, stale or compressed context, instruction misunderstandings, environmental changes, and accumulated state errors. Trace concrete failure chains from initiating fault through subsequent actions to user-visible consequences; distinguish model limitations from architecture, orchestration, memory, interface, and environment failures. Investigate detection of silent errors, calibrated uncertainty versus actual failure, retry and replanning policies, escalation, and safe termination. Analyze checkpointing, state reconstruction, independent verification, rollback, idempotency, and human intervention as recovery mechanisms. For each mechanism, specify assumptions, failure modes, and measurable recovery criteria; compare recovery against restarting and continuing without intervention. Develop fault-injection scenarios and trace-based analyses that reveal propagation and test whether recovery restores correct state rather than merely producing a plausible answer. Deliver a failure taxonomy, causal workflow maps, and a prioritized set of falsifiable experiments, distinguishing observed evidence from proposed mechanisms.

strategy_snapshot.title: Develop a rigorous framework for measuring AI agent reliability
Understand failure propagation and recovery in autonomous AI agents
Test architectural mechanisms for dependable agent outcomes

problem:
Autonomous AI agents are increasingly expected to complete complex tasks involving planning, reasoning, external tools, persistent state, and interaction with changing environments. Demonstrations and benchmark results show that agents can perform many such tasks, but provide limited evidence that they remain dependable across repeated executions, unfamiliar conditions, long-running workflows, and settings where mistakes have significant consequences. This project asks how autonomous and semi-autonomous agents can be evaluated and engineered to deliver reliable, correct, recoverable, and reproducible results across extended, multi-step tasks.

Agent reliability is a system-level property. Probabilistic decisions, dynamically constructed plans, incomplete observations, tool interfaces, memory, orchestration, and external state all affect whether the intended outcome is actually achieved. Small errors can propagate through later actions and yield plausible but incorrect results. An agent may claim completion without satisfying the task, recover from one failure while introducing another, or behave differently across otherwise comparable runs. Reliability therefore cannot be inferred from fluent explanations, a single successful trajectory, agreement among similar models, or benchmark scores alone.

Investigate three connected questions. First, how should reliability be defined and measured so evaluation reflects actual correctness, robustness, consistency, recoverability, tool-use quality, and cost rather than superficial completion? Second, what are the principal sources of failure, how do errors propagate through multi-step execution, and which signals and interventions can detect, contain, or recover from failures without creating additional risks? Third, which engineering mechanisms demonstrably improve outcomes, and how can their effects be established through controlled experiments rather than architectural intuition or anecdotal success? The strategies approach these questions from complementary measurement, failure-analysis, and intervention perspectives; none presumes a preferred architecture.

Use available research literature, software-reliability principles, empirical evaluation methods, and documented agent-system designs. Examine the relationship between model capability and end-to-end system reliability, including tool interfaces, state management, verification, orchestration, uncertainty handling, changing environments, recovery, and execution budgets. Assess benchmark sensitivity to task selection, evaluator bias, contamination, and weak completion oracles. Consider stochastic behavior, repeated trials, long dependency chains, held-out tasks, fault injection, independent correctness judgments, and uncertainty in estimated success rates. Where comparisons are proposed, make assumptions and controls explicit, including model and prompt versions, task difficulty, environment, tool access, compute, latency, and monetary budgets.

Evaluate competing approaches on the strength and limits of their evidence. Distinguish measured results from formal or theoretical arguments, proposed mechanisms, and unsupported claims; do not present planned experiments as completed or infer causal benefit from correlation. Account for correlated errors among agents or critics that share models and training data, and for the difficulty of constructing an independent oracle for open-ended tasks. Analyze tradeoffs among reliability, flexibility, recovery overhead, latency, and computational expense, including cases where a safeguard shifts rather than removes risk.

The intended outcome is an evidence-grounded account of what reliability claims current evaluations can support, a practical and reproducible evaluation framework, a causal taxonomy of important failure and recovery modes, and architectural principles whose limits are explicit. Identify unresolved questions and specify discriminating experiments needed to validate competing claims. The project is open-ended: conclusions should remain proportional to the quality, independence, and generality of available evidence.

output.claim: A reliability lower bound can explicitly allow an imperfect reference judge without assuming that judge errors are independent of agent or automated-evaluator errors. Let Y denote true execution success, O automated acceptance, and R reference certification. If Pr(O=1,R=1,Y=0)≤η, then true reliability p=Pr(Y=1) satisfies p≥max(0,Pr(O=1)−Pr(O=1,R=0)−η). This population bound is sharp under precisely this error allowance. A cluster-level finite-sample version remains valid under arbitrary dependence among repeated runs of the same task. Without a justified allowance η, even perfect agreement between O and R cannot certify positive true reliability.
output.method: Develop a standalone conditional lemma addressing the ledger's unresolved reference-error allowance, rather than reconstructing the unavailable earlier proof. Hypothesis: evaluator agreement alone does not identify correctness, whereas an explicit bound on jointly accepted failures supports a conservative reliability guarantee. The discriminating analytical outcomes are a sharp lower bound, an observationally indistinguishable failure example, and a confidence bound that counts independent tasks rather than repeated runs as independent units. Assumptions and target population are specified below. The proposed next empirical test is a repeated-panel coverage experiment with correlated within-task outcomes and shared judge errors; it has not been executed because both runtimes are unavailable. The original artifact df5067f1-d298-4203-a108-a2e7056af576 is pointer-only, so its proof and counterexample have not been inspected. Its ledger entries supply priorities, not certified premises. The truncated extract 984e8fd3-f76b-46fb-b868-378c2f103425 concerns ambiguous external commits; its restricted recovery model does not establish a measurement bound and is not transferred here. Recorded provider failures, interruption, and timeout are operational metadata, not mathematical evidence; this action is a bounded analytical derivation rather than a repeated execution request.

reasoning_steps.title: Define the target and the reference-error allowance
reasoning_steps.argument: Fix an execution protocol, task distribution D, resource budget, observation horizon, and binary success rubric. For a randomly drawn task, execute a batch of r≥1 runs and select one run uniformly. Define Y, O, R∈{0,1} for that execution: actual rubric satisfaction, automated acceptance, and reference certification. Set p=Pr(Y=1), q=Pr(O=1), a=Pr(O=1,R=0), and c=Pr(O=1,R=1,Y=0). Assume c≤η for a prespecified η∈[0,1]. This is an unconditional probability over the target execution population, not the conditional error rate Pr(Y=0|R=1). A valid bound on Pr(R=1,Y=0) would also bound c, but is stronger than required.

reasoning_steps.title: Derive the population reliability bound
reasoning_steps.argument: Partition accepted executions by reference outcome. Accepted failures satisfy Pr(O=1,Y=0)=Pr(O=1,R=0,Y=0)+c≤a+η. Also p≥Pr(O=1,Y=1)=q−Pr(O=1,Y=0). Combining gives p≥q−a−η, and p≥0 gives the stated clipped bound. No independence of Y, O, and R was used. False reference rejection may make a unnecessarily large and the bound conservative, but does not invalidate it.

reasoning_steps.title: Establish sharpness and boundary cases
reasoning_steps.argument: Write s=Pr(O=1,R=1)=q−a, where 0≤a≤q≤1. Keeping any feasible joint distribution of (O,R) fixed, assign Y=0 everywhere outside the event {O=1,R=1}. Within that event, assign failure probability mass min(s,η) and success mass max(0,s−η). This yields c=min(s,η)≤η and p=max(0,s−η), attaining the lower bound. Assigning Y=1 everywhere attains p=1 under the same observed (O,R) distribution. Mixtures preserve the observed distribution and error allowance, filling the interval between these extremes. Thus the identified interval is [max(0,q−a−η),1] when this localized error allowance is the only constraint involving Y. This includes s=0, η=0, and η≥s. Additional truth constraints could narrow the interval.

reasoning_steps.title: Show why judge agreement cannot calibrate the allowance
reasoning_steps.argument: Consider O=R=1 on every execution. A world with Y=1 always and a world with Y=0 always have identical observed judge outputs, but p equals one and zero respectively. The second world has c=1. Therefore agreement data alone cannot establish a small η; any argument excluding the second world needs information connecting judgments to actual outcomes. More judges that always share these outputs do not remove the ambiguity. This is an identification counterexample, not an observed failure rate for any agent benchmark.

reasoning_steps.title: Construct independent-task estimators
reasoning_steps.argument: For N evaluation task clusters, let X_i=(1/r)Σ_j O_ij and q_hat=(1/N)Σ_i X_i. Assume the clusters are independent and identically distributed under the fixed protocol; dependence within each batch is unrestricted. Then X_i∈[0,1] and E[X_i]=q by uniform run selection. Separately draw m independent audit task clusters from the same D, execute the same r-run protocol, and select one run uniformly from each batch. For its labels define Z_k=1{O=1,R=0}; a_hat=(1/m)Σ_k Z_k has expectation a. Audit selection must not condition on automated acceptance. This construction never treats the Nr executions as Nr independent observations.

reasoning_steps.title: Derive finite-sample coverage
reasoning_steps.argument: For independent [0,1]-valued observations W_i, the bounded-variable exponential-moment inequality gives E exp(λΣ_i(W_i−EW_i))≤exp(nλ²/8). Markov's inequality, minimized at λ=4t, therefore gives Pr(mean(W)−E mean(W)≥t)≤exp(−2nt²); applying it to −W gives the opposite tail. For 0<α<1 set t_N=sqrt(log(2/α)/(2N)) and t_m=sqrt(log(2/α)/(2m)). Hence q≥q_hat−t_N and a≤a_hat+t_m simultaneously with probability at least 1−α by a union bound. Substitution into the population inequality proves that L=max(0,q_hat−t_N−a_hat−t_m−η) satisfies Pr(p≥L)≥1−α, conditional on the population error allowance and sampling assumptions. The union bound does not require independence between the two estimation errors, although the stated sampling design supplies independent panels.

reasoning_steps.title: Separate a sensitivity parameter from a validated guarantee
reasoning_steps.argument: If η is only a hypothetical sensitivity value, L is only a conditional sensitivity result. If a separate valid procedure supplies an upper confidence bound η_U for c with failure probability at most β, replacing η by η_U yields coverage at least 1−α−β by another union bound, without requiring independence of procedures. A third judge's agreement is not itself such a procedure. With no defensible restriction on c, η=1 is always valid and L=0; the framework then honestly provides no positive reliability certificate. Separate estimation of q and a is one sufficient construction, not a universal requirement: direct truth evaluation or a joint estimator could be preferable when available.

reasoning_steps.title: Specify the discriminating validation test
reasoning_steps.argument: A proposed implementation test should generate independent task clusters with easy/hard heterogeneity, varying within-task correlation, and a shared judge-error mechanism controlling c. Across repeated panels and several N, m, and r values, compare the frequency L>p against α when the allowance is valid. Include η=0 with perfect reference certification, η=c, a deliberately understated η<c, and perfectly correlated repeated runs. Retain a naive run-independent interval only as a negative control, not as an endorsed method. Ground truth and population probabilities should be known from the finite generative model or derived independently. Such finite tests would check implementation and sensitivity, not prove the coverage theorem or demonstrate real-agent reliability.

assumptions: The task distribution, execution protocol, versions, resource budgets, success rubric, observation horizon, and sampling plan are fixed before examining outcomes; p concerns this protocol only.
Y correctly represents actual rubric satisfaction. It need not be observed in routine evaluation, but evidence bounding reference miscertification must ultimately connect to actual outcomes.
The target-population probability c=Pr(O=1,R=1,Y=0) is at most the stated η. This premise is not established by the available evidence.

Evaluation task clusters are independently and identically sampled, with independent cluster-level execution randomness and no unmodeled shared persistent state. Within-task run dependence is unrestricted.

output.claim: In the state machine specified below, atomic durable coupling of an external effect and its completed deduplication record preserves at-most-one effect per stable operation key through crashes and delayed duplicate deliveries. It yields exactly one effect if at least one matching request eventually completes its commit transition. Merely writing the effect and the record separately does not provide this guarantee: explicit crash traces produce either duplicate effects or a false completed record with no effect. These are conditional analytical results and manually derived test expectations, not executed agent experiments.
output.method: Specify separate durable business state, deduplication state, agent state, network state, and evaluator-only traces; derive invariants and counterexample traces from their transitions. Hypothesis for a subsequent experiment: atomic deduplication prevents ambiguous-commit duplication when identity is preserved, whereas checkpoint restoration or a separate completed-key table alone does not. The discriminating outcomes are independently audited effects, effect-record correspondence, and outstanding requests after recovery—not completion language. First audit the deterministic harness against the trace suite; only then compare real agent recovery policies under matched fault schedules, initial snapshots, model/prompt/tool versions, and budget caps. Include no-fault controls and distinguish dropped requests from delayed requests. No runtime is available, so no implementation or experiment was executed. The bounded specification responds to the earlier timeout and interrupted review without repeating a failed execution request. The supplied prior extract motivates the question but is incomplete; the argument below is derived explicitly rather than treating its repair claim as certified.

reasoning_steps.title: Define the state and correctness boundary
reasoning_steps.argument: Let S=(E,D,L,Q,V,J). E is a durable multiset of actual business effects, each containing an effect identifier, operation key k, and full payload p. D is a durable map from k to a completed record (p,result,effect_identifier). L is the agent's durable intent/checkpoint and visible transcript. Q contains pending request and acknowledgment envelopes, each with a distinct delivery identifier. V is volatile service execution state. J is an evaluator-only event journal. For one intended operation (k,p), task correctness requires exactly one effect with that key and payload, and no unintended effect. A completed D entry is an assertion of completion, not the outcome oracle. The evaluator reads E directly and audits its correspondence with D. This intentionally narrow ledger-backed task does not supply an oracle for open-ended agent work.

reasoning_steps.title: Specify failure and observation semantics
reasoning_steps.argument: SEND adds a request (delivery_id,k,p) to Q without changing E or D. DROP permanently removes an envelope before processing; DELAY leaves it eligible for later processing. A service crash discards V but preserves E and D; it does not implicitly cancel network envelopes. Agent restore changes L to its checkpoint but cannot change E,D, or Q. Acknowledgments are separately enqueued and delivered or dropped. Every transition is recorded in J. The agent observes only its configured projection: L, delivered tool messages, and a controlled logical clock. It cannot inspect E,D,Q,J or hidden service metadata in the local-only arm. This restriction must be enforced and audited in an implementation; it is not an assertion about ordinary deployed tools.

reasoning_steps.title: Define atomic processing and prove its safety invariant
reasoning_steps.argument: An atomic PROCESS(k,p) transition behaves as follows. If D[k] is absent, it simultaneously appends one effect e=(id,k,p) to E and installs D[k]=(p,result,id). If D[k] contains the same full payload, it returns the recorded result without changing E or D. If the payload differs, it rejects without an effect. A crash during the atomic transition exposes either its entire before-state or its entire after-state. Starting with E=D=empty, the invariant is: for each key, either D is absent and no effect exists, or D identifies exactly one matching effect and no other effect exists for that key. Induction proves it: an absent-key transition creates precisely the matching pair; replay and rejection preserve it; SEND, DROP, DELAY, acknowledgment handling, and crashes do not alter the pair. Atomic serialization covers simultaneous requests, so both cannot observe an absent key at their commit points. Thus any finite sequence, including delayed duplicate deliveries, preserves at-most-one effect.

reasoning_steps.title: Separate safety, eventual effect, and verified completion
reasoning_steps.argument: The invariant does not imply that an effect ever occurs: all requests might be dropped, or execution might stop before processing. If at least one matching request completes PROCESS, its absent-key branch creates one effect or its replay branch witnesses an existing matching effect. Combining this existence argument with at-most-one gives exactly one effect. An acknowledgment need not reach the agent, so actual correctness does not imply verified completion. Conversely, a finite-time observation of one effect need not establish stable success when a non-deduplicated request remains pending. Final audits must drain all accepted requests under a declared schedule or establish that they have been irrevocably fenced; a timeout alone is not such a fence.

reasoning_steps.title: Manually derive the ordinary-operation ambiguity controls
reasoning_steps.argument: Write a summary state as (N,d,q), where N counts intended-key effects, d=1 means a completed D entry exists, and q counts outstanding requests; omitted acknowledgments are stated separately. In ordinary mode, processing always appends an effect and leaves D empty. T0, no fault: SEND; PROCESS; deliver acknowledgment gives (1,0,0) and visible success. T1, pre-commit loss: SEND; DROP; timeout gives (0,0,0). T2, post-commit acknowledgment loss: SEND; PROCESS; DROP acknowledgment; timeout gives (1,0,0). Restore the same intent checkpoint and expose the same logical-time timeout transcript in T1 and T2. Their agent projections must then be byte-for-byte equal despite different E. Skipping leaves effect counts 0 and 1 respectively; issuing one successfully processed retry leaves counts 1 and 2. This reproduces the relevant ambiguity without assuming an implemented harness already hides every side channel.

reasoning_steps.title: Manually derive atomic recovery and crash traces
reasoning_steps.argument: T3, atomic pre-commit loss: SEND; DROP; timeout; restore; SEND same (k,p); PROCESS gives (1,1,0). T4, atomic post-commit acknowledgment loss: SEND; PROCESS; DROP acknowledgment; timeout; restore; retry same (k,p); PROCESS leaves (1,1,0), and the returned effect identifier equals the original identifier. T5, crash immediately before the atomic commit leaves (0,0,0) after the consumed request is lost; retry creates (1,1,0). Crash immediately after commit but before acknowledgment instead leaves (1,1,0); retry preserves it. The required checks are the full payload, effect identifier, record-effect correspondence, and invariant after every transition, not merely the final count. These are consequences of the atomic model, not evidence that a specific service implements it.

reasoning_steps.title: Give counterexample traces for separately written completed records
reasoning_steps.argument: Consider a deliberately unsafe handler that checks D and, if absent, performs two durable writes without a recovery protocol. T6, effect first: append effect gives (1,0,0); crash before writing D; retry sees no record and appends another effect, then writes D, giving (2,1,0). T7, record first: write a completed record containing a reserved effect identifier, giving (0,1,0); crash before creating that effect; retry treats D as completed and returns success without an effect, leaving (0,1,0). T6 violates at-most-one; T7 violates completed-record soundness and exactly-one. Both failures occur with stable key and payload. These traces refute sufficiency of this naive two-write handler, not all non-atomic implementations: a pending-state protocol with durable recovery, fencing, or downstream deduplication requires separate analysis.

reasoning_steps.title: Expose the delayed-request hazard and the limit of lookup
reasoning_steps.argument: T8: SEND request a; DELAY a; timeout gives (0,0,1). An authoritative lookup now correctly reports no effect. SEND retry b; process b gives (1,0,1); process delayed a gives (2,0,0) in ordinary mode. Thus even a correct lookup of current state is not sufficient to justify a non-idempotent retry when earlier requests remain live. In atomic mode with the same key and payload, the corresponding suffix is (1,1,1) then (1,1,0), because a becomes a replay. Skipping after the timeout also need not mean permanent failure: releasing a can eventually produce one effect. Consequently delayed and dropped requests must be distinct experimental strata. The earlier forced skip-or-one-retry bound must not be transferred unchanged to lookup or pending-request policies.

reasoning_steps.title: Specify negative controls that test the repair assumptions
reasoning_steps.argument: T9, identity drift: after an atomic commit and lost acknowledgment, retry using a fresh key k2; both keys are absent on their first commits, so two effects occur for the same user intention even though per-key invariants hold. T10, payload drift: retry the original key with p2 different from p; the specified atomic handler rejects and leaves E unchanged. T11, retention failure: commit, delete D[k] while retaining E, then retry; the absent-key branch produces a second effect. T12, concurrency: queue two identical requests before processing either; the atomic model yields one effect regardless of their order. A split implementation that lets both workers read absent before either writes can create two. reasoning_steps.title: Define the state and observation boundary
reasoning_steps.argument: One intended business operation has key k and exact canonical payload p. Durable business state E is an append-only collection of effect entries; N is the number attributable to this intended operation, including erroneous retries under another key. Durable service map D stores k -> (p, effect identifier, result). Durable agent checkpoint C stores the intended k and p. Network state Q contains pending requests and responses. Volatile service state V contains incomplete handlers. Evaluator-only log L records delivery, commit, crash, and response events. The agent observes only C and its tool-visible transcript O, not E, D, Q, V, or L. Attribution metadata used by the evaluator is not an extra service deduplication mechanism. Correctness is N=1; receipt of a success response is a separate observable.

reasoning_steps.title: Specify delivery, ordinary execution, and crash transitions
reasoning_steps.argument: Send adds a request to Q. Drop permanently removes it before execution; delay leaves it in Q and permits later delivery. A timeout changes O but neither cancels Q nor establishes that execution failed. The ordinary service appends one effect for each delivered valid request and then enqueues a response. Dropping a response does not undo an effect. A service crash clears V but preserves E and D; it does not implicitly cancel network requests. An agent restart restores C and the specified checkpoint-visible transcript. At the audit horizon, pending requests must be reported; final effect correctness is assessed after draining the finite test schedule or establishing a real cancellation barrier, not merely after an agent timeout.

reasoning_steps.title: Specify the atomic deduplicating alternative
reasoning_steps.argument: For a delivered request (k,p), the atomic service performs one serializable durable transition. If k is absent, it appends one effect and installs D[k]=(p,id,result) together. If k is present with identical p, it changes neither E nor D and returns the stored result. If k is present with different p, it rejects without an effect. Concurrent handlers for the same key are serialized at this transition. A crash can leave either the complete pre-transition state or the complete post-transition state, never one write alone. A response is generated only after the durable transition. No records expire during the retry and delayed-delivery horizon. This specifies a transactional boundary around the actual business effect, not just a local record describing a separate external action.

reasoning_steps.title: Derive safety and separate it from progress
reasoning_steps.argument: Initially E and D are empty for k. Inductively, a first atomic insertion creates exactly one effect paired with one matching record. Every later matching request is read-only; mismatching requests reject; drops, timeouts, and crashes cannot change the durable pair. Thus D[k] exists if and only if exactly one corresponding effect exists, and that effect matches its stored payload and identifier. Therefore N<=1 for the intended operation if every attempt preserves its unique k and p. If at least one valid request eventually completes the atomic transition, the absent-key branch creates an effect or the present-key branch witnesses an existing one, so N=1. Without that delivery/commit premise, perpetual dropping leaves N=0. Even with N=1, the agent need not know completion if every response is lost.

reasoning_steps.title: Derive baseline traces and distinguish delay from loss
reasoning_steps.argument: Each trace starts fresh at N=0. T1, ordinary no fault: deliver original, append, deliver acknowledgment -> N=1. T2, ordinary pre-commit drop: drop original, timeout, deliver retry -> N=1. T3, ordinary lost acknowledgment: deliver original and append, drop acknowledgment, timeout, deliver retry -> N=2. T4, ordinary delayed original: hold original, timeout, deliver retry and append, then release original and append -> N=2. Restoring the same local checkpoint changes none of these counts. T2 and T3 can have exactly the same agent-visible recovery prefix by construction despite different external states. T4 shows why treating all timeouts as permanent drops would invalidate the test.

reasoning_steps.title: Derive atomic-service traces, including crash boundaries
reasoning_steps.argument: Write states as (N, number of records for k). T5, atomic pre-commit drop followed by delivered retry: (0,0)->(1,1). T6, atomic original commit with lost acknowledgment followed by matching retry: (0,0)->(1,1)->(1,1). T7, delayed original released after the matching retry, or two concurrent matching deliveries: serialization gives (0,0)->(1,1)->(1,1), regardless of delivery order. T8, crash at the atomic transition: the recovered state is either (0,0) or (1,1); a subsequently delivered matching retry ends at (1,1) in either case. The mixed states (1,0) and (0,1) are forbidden observations for this implementation. Acknowledgment loss affects knowledge, not these durable counts.

reasoning_steps.title: Construct counterexamples to separately written key tables
reasoning_steps.argument: T9, effect-first implementation: append effect -> (1,0), crash before writing the key record, recover, retry sees no record and appends again, then writes the record -> (2,1). T10, record-first implementation with a record treated as completed: install record -> (0,1), crash before effect, recover, retry returns the cached completion and performs no effect -> (0,1). These are counterexamples to those two explicitly defined naive implementations, not to all non-atomic protocols. A pending-record protocol with reconciliation has different transitions and needs a separate proof; labeling a record 'pending' alone does not establish that proof.

reasoning_steps.title: Specify assumption-breaking controls
reasoning_steps.argument: T11, after an atomic success retry with the same k but a different payload: rejection must leave (1,1), and the mismatch must be observable to the agent. T12, retry the same intended operation with a new key: the service legitimately inserts another record and effect, so total N=2; this tests agent identity preservation, not a violation of per-key atomicity. T13, delete the original record after success while retaining its effect, then deliver a matching retry: a fresh insertion produces N=2. This demonstrates the retention requirement. Also reuse a key for two genuinely distinct intended operations: the second may be suppressed or rejected, showing why uniqueness across operations matters. These controls make scope violations visible instead of counting them as unexplained regressions.

reasoning_steps.title: Define the audit contract and causal comparison
reasoning_steps.argument: For every trace, retain full evaluator event order, durable snapshots at each crash boundary, final effect-to-intent attribution, request key/payload lineage, response content, pending requests, and the exact actor-visible recovery prefix. The H0/H1 indistinguishability assertion requires equality of every actor-accessible field before the recovery decision, including timing, tool metadata, restored memory, and status channels; evaluator-only differences are allowed. Begin with scripted identical retry behavior to isolate service semantics, then hold service semantics fixed while testing whether real agents preserve identity across restart and replanning. Use no-fault runs to expose overhead and regressions. Report all-run verified success, duplicate/missing effects, false completion, unresolved outcomes, latency, tool use, and cost separately. Scripted trace agreement validates only those traces; repeated agent trials and held-out workflows are still required for an architectural benefit claim.

output.method: Refine only the request lifecycle and manually evaluate the affected traces from empty durable state. The specification hypothesis is that explicitly separating dequeue, durable processing, and acknowledgment enqueue makes every request's fate determinate without changing the atomic E/D safety argument. The discriminating checks are delivery-ID conservation, exact pending and terminal request locations, and effect-record correspondence after every event. reasoning_steps.title: State, identifiers, and table notation
reasoning_steps.argument: Retain S=(E,D,L,Q,V,J) from the supplied extract of artifact 4435b6ec-fefc-43a1-8706-a3a6794dbbe5. E is the durable effect multiset; D is the durable completed-record map; L is agent state; J is evaluator-only event history. Partition Q into request envelopes Q_R and acknowledgment envelopes Q_A. A request is (x,k,p), where delivery ID x is globally fresh, independently of stable operation key k. An acknowledgment has a fresh envelope ID alpha_x, correlation field x, and the processing outcome. Retries use a new delivery ID but the same k,p. Q is an independently maintained network-envelope pool: it survives service crashes but permits explicit DROP. It is not a durable broker with automatic redelivery. V contains a service up/down flag and volatile workers xR=(x,k,p,ready) or xC=(x,k,p,processed,outcome). Multiple workers are allowed. Tables display worker entries only; CRASH makes the service down and RESTART makes it up. '-' means empty. T is an evaluator-only terminal-request map derived from J, not additional recoverable service state: L0=lost before processing, L1=processed but reply lost before enqueue, F=handler finished with acknowledgment enqueued, X=explicitly dropped from Q_R. Each trace starts with empty E,D,Q,V,T and an up service.

reasoning_steps.title: SEND, RECEIVE, delay, and drop
reasoning_steps.argument: SEND(x,k,p) adds exactly one fresh request envelope x to Q_R. RECEIVE(x) requires an up service and an eligible x in Q_R; it atomically removes x from Q_R and installs xR in V. RECEIVE changes neither E nor D and creates no acknowledgment. No copy or lease for x remains in Q. DELAY(x) makes no location change and merely withholds its RECEIVE until release. DROP(x) removes x from Q_R and records T[x]=X; dropping an acknowledgment instead removes its envelope from Q_A and records that acknowledgment's loss in J. A timeout does not remove an envelope or worker. Agent restore changes L only. There is no implicit duplicate delivery: an explicit retry is a new SEND with a fresh delivery ID.

reasoning_steps.title: PROCESS is separate from acknowledgment enqueue
reasoning_steps.argument: PROCESS(x) requires xR and an up service. In atomic mode, it tests current D at the serialized processing point, not at RECEIVE. If D[k] is absent, it atomically appends e=(effect_id,k,p) to E and installs D[k]=(p,result,effect_id). If D[k] matches p, it leaves E,D unchanged and obtains the recorded result and effect ID. If the payload differs, it leaves E,D unchanged and obtains a mismatch rejection. The transition replaces xR with xC carrying that outcome; x remains absent from Q_R. ACK_ENQUEUE(x) requires xC, inserts alpha_x into Q_A, removes xC from V, and records T[x]=F. This enqueue/removal is one abstract transition, so it cannot emit two acknowledgments for one worker. ACK_DELIVER(alpha_x) removes that envelope from Q_A, appends its correlated response to L, and records delivery in J. It does not change T[x], E, or D. For the ordinary control, PROCESS always appends a fresh effect and leaves D empty, then creates xC in the same way.

reasoning_steps.title: Crash boundary and request accounting
reasoning_steps.argument: CRASH clears every worker from V and sets the service down. For each xR it records T[x]=L0; for each xC it records T[x]=L1. It preserves E,D,Q_R,Q_A,L and prior terminal records. RESTART sets the service up with no workers; it reconstructs no consumed delivery. Thus a crash before RECEIVE leaves x queued, a crash after RECEIVE but before PROCESS loses x without an effect, a crash after PROCESS but before ACK_ENQUEUE loses only the volatile reply, and a crash after ACK_ENQUEUE leaves alpha_x pending in Q_A. A crash concurrent with atomic PROCESS is represented by either its before-state followed by CRASH or its complete after-state followed by CRASH; a partial E/D write is excluded by premise. The sent request IDs partition disjointly into Q_R, worker IDs in V, and terminal IDs in T. SEND introduces one ID, RECEIVE transfers it, PROCESS changes its worker phase, and enqueue/drop/crash transfers it to T. This proves complete request accounting inductively. Ack IDs similarly partition into Q_A and the delivered/dropped acknowledgment events in J. No automatic redelivery occurs after a pre-commit crash in this model; durable lease/redelivery semantics would be a different model.

reasoning_steps.title: Durable invariant and ledger abbreviations
reasoning_steps.argument: For each key, invariant I is: either D[k] is absent and E contains no effect for k, or D[k]=(p,r,id) and E contains exactly one effect for k, namely (id,k,p), whose recorded result is r. Define Z=(E=empty,D=empty). Define P_x=(E={e_x},D[k]=(p,r_x,id_x)), with e_x=(id_x,k,p) created by delivery x. Define O_b=(E={e_b},D=empty) and O_ba=(E={e_b,e_a},D=empty) for the ordinary control. Z and every P_x satisfy I, including full payload and identifier correspondence, not just counts. O_b and O_ba fail I because ordinary mode intentionally has no D record; O_b still has at-most-one effect, whereas O_ba does not. In atomic mode, first PROCESS creates one matching pair, replay/rejection preserve it, and every other lifecycle transition leaves E,D unchanged. This proves I from empty initialization despite crashes and concurrent workers. It supplies safety only: loss of every ready worker can leave Z forever.

reasoning_steps.argument:
All requests below carry the same k,p. Each row is the state after the named event. Every durable state is Z or P_b, so I holds on every row.

reasoning_steps.title: Define the target and the reference-error allowance
reasoning_steps.argument: Fix an execution protocol, task distribution D, resource budget, observation horizon, and binary success rubric. For a randomly drawn task, execute a batch of r≥1 runs and select one run uniformly. Define Y, O, R∈{0,1} for that execution: actual rubric satisfaction, automated acceptance, and reference certification. Set p=Pr(Y=1), q=Pr(O=1), a=Pr(O=1,R=0), and c=Pr(O=1,R=1,Y=0). Assume c≤η for a prespecified η∈[0,1]. This is an unconditional probability over the target execution population, not the conditional error rate Pr(Y=0|R=1). A valid bound on Pr(R=1,Y=0) would also bound c, but is stronger than required.

reasoning_steps.title: Derive the population reliability bound
reasoning_steps.argument: Partition accepted executions by reference outcome. Accepted failures satisfy Pr(O=1,Y=0)=Pr(O=1,R=0,Y=0)+c≤a+η. Also p≥Pr(O=1,Y=1)=q−Pr(O=1,Y=0). Combining gives p≥q−a−η, and p≥0 gives the stated clipped bound. No independence of Y, O, and R was used. False reference rejection may make a unnecessarily large and the bound conservative, but does not invalidate it.

reasoning_steps.title: Establish sharpness and boundary cases
reasoning_steps.argument: Write s=Pr(O=1,R=1)=q−a, where 0≤a≤q≤1. Keeping any feasible joint distribution of (O,R) fixed, assign Y=0 everywhere outside the event {O=1,R=1}. Within that event, assign failure probability mass min(s,η) and success mass max(0,s−η). This yields c=min(s,η)≤η and p=max(0,s−η), attaining the lower bound. Assigning Y=1 everywhere attains p=1 under the same observed (O,R) distribution. Mixtures preserve the observed distribution and error allowance, filling the interval between these extremes. Thus the identified interval is [max(0,q−a−η),1] when this localized error allowance is the only constraint involving Y. This includes s=0, η=0, and η≥s. Additional truth constraints could narrow the interval.

reasoning_steps.title: Show why judge agreement cannot calibrate the allowance
reasoning_steps.argument: Consider O=R=1 on every execution. A world with Y=1 always and a world with Y=0 always have identical observed judge outputs, but p equals one and zero respectively. The second world has c=1. Therefore agreement data alone cannot establish a small η; any argument excluding the second world needs information connecting judgments to actual outcomes. More judges that always share these outputs do not remove the ambiguity. This is an identification counterexample, not an observed failure rate for any agent benchmark.

reasoning_steps.title: Construct independent-task estimators
reasoning_steps.argument: For N evaluation task clusters, let X_i=(1/r)Σ_j O_ij and q_hat=(1/N)Σ_i X_i. Assume the clusters are independent and identically distributed under the fixed protocol; dependence within each batch is unrestricted. Then X_i∈[0,1] and E[X_i]=q by uniform run selection. Separately draw m independent audit task clusters from the same D, execute the same r-run protocol, and select one run uniformly from each batch. For its labels define Z_k=1{O=1,R=0}; a_hat=(1/m)Σ_k Z_k has expectation a. Audit selection must not condition on automated acceptance. This construction never treats the Nr executions as Nr independent observations.

reasoning_steps.title: Derive finite-sample coverage

Independent bounded task-cluster averages support one-sided concentration; allocating α/2 to each estimator and applying a union bound establishes coverage. A further confidence allowance for c can be incorporated with an additional failure-probability allocation.

argument_steps.title: Define the target and the reference-error allowance
argument_steps.argument: Fix an execution protocol, task distribution D, resource budget, observation horizon, and binary success rubric. For a randomly drawn task, execute a batch of r≥1 runs and select one run uniformly. Define Y, O, R∈{0,1} for that execution: actual rubric satisfaction, automated acceptance, and reference certification. Set p=Pr(Y=1), q=Pr(O=1), a=Pr(O=1,R=0), and c=Pr(O=1,R=1,Y=0). Assume c≤η for a prespecified η∈[0,1]. This is an unconditional probability over the target execution population, not the conditional error rate Pr(Y=0|R=1). A valid bound on Pr(R=1,Y=0) would also bound c, but is stronger than required.

review.rationale: Uniform selection within a fixed r-run batch defines a coherent marginal execution population. The localized unconditional error probability c differs correctly from a conditional reference-error rate. The allowance is accepted only as an explicit premise of the conditional claim.

argument_steps.title: Derive the population reliability bound
argument_steps.argument: Partition accepted executions by reference outcome. Accepted failures satisfy Pr(O=1,Y=0)=Pr(O=1,R=0,Y=0)+c≤a+η. Also p≥Pr(O=1,Y=1)=q−Pr(O=1,Y=0). Combining gives p≥q−a−η, and p≥0 gives the stated clipped bound. No independence of Y, O, and R was used. False reference rejection may make a unnecessarily large and the bound conservative, but does not invalidate it.

review.rationale: Partitioning accepted failures by R gives Pr(O=1,Y=0)≤a+c≤a+η. Accepted true successes form a subset of all true successes, so subtraction from q and clipping at zero establish the bound without judge independence.

argument_steps.title: Establish sharpness and boundary cases
argument_steps.argument: Write s=Pr(O=1,R=1)=q−a, where 0≤a≤q≤1. Keeping any feasible joint distribution of (O,R) fixed, assign Y=0 everywhere outside the event {O=1,R=1}. Within that event, assign failure probability mass min(s,η) and success mass max(0,s−η). This yields c=min(s,η)≤η and p=max(0,s−η), attaining the lower bound. Assigning Y=1 everywhere attains p=1 under the same observed (O,R) distribution. Mixtures preserve the observed distribution and error allowance, filling the interval between these extremes. Thus the identified interval is [max(0,q−a−η),1] when this localized error allowance is the only constraint involving Y. This includes s=0, η=0, and η≥s. Additional truth constraints could narrow the interval.

review.rationale: For any feasible observed joint distribution, setting truth to failure outside the jointly accepted cell and allocating min(s,η) failure mass inside it attains max(0,s−η). Universal success is also feasible. Mixtures preserve observations and the inequality on c, establishing every intermediate reliability value.

argument_steps.title: Show why judge agreement cannot calibrate the allowance
argument_steps.argument: Consider O=R=1 on every execution. A world with Y=1 always and a world with Y=0 always have identical observed judge outputs, but p equals one and zero respectively. The second world has c=1. Therefore agreement data alone cannot establish a small η; any argument excluding the second world needs information connecting judgments to actual outcomes. More judges that always share these outputs do not remove the ambiguity. This is an identification counterexample, not an observed failure rate for any agent benchmark.

review.rationale: The two worlds have identical observed judge outputs but different truth labels and reliabilities. This establishes nonidentification from agreement alone, not an empirical benchmark failure rate or a contradiction to a separately justified η<1.

argument_steps.title: Construct independent-task estimators
argument_steps.argument: For N evaluation task clusters, let X_i=(1/r)Σ_j O_ij and q_hat=(1/N)Σ_i X_i. Assume the clusters are independent and identically distributed under the fixed protocol; dependence within each batch is unrestricted. Then X_i∈[0,1] and E[X_i]=q by uniform run selection. Separately draw m independent audit task clusters from the same D, execute the same r-run protocol, and select one run uniformly from each batch. For its labels define Z_k=1{O=1,R=0}; a_hat=(1/m)Σ_k Z_k has expectation a. Audit selection must not condition on automated acceptance. This construction never treats the Nr executions as Nr independent observations.

review.rationale: Averaging the run-specific acceptance probabilities equals the probability for a uniformly selected run, so E[X_i]=q despite within-batch dependence. Uniform unconditioned audit selection similarly gives E[Z_k]=a. The assumptions match the conditional claim; acceptance-conditioned auditing would require a different weighted estimator.

argument_steps.title: Derive finite-sample coverage
argument_steps.argument: For independent [0,1]-valued observations W_i, the bounded-variable exponential-moment inequality gives E exp(λΣ_i(W_i−EW_i))≤exp(nλ²/8). Markov's inequality, minimized at λ=4t, therefore gives Pr(mean(W)−E mean(W)≥t)≤exp(−2nt²); applying it to −W gives the opposite tail. For 0<α<1 set t_N=sqrt(log(2/α)/(2N)) and t_m=sqrt(log(2/α)/(2m)). Hence q≥q_hat−t_N and a≤a_hat+t_m simultaneously with probability at least 1−α by a union bound. Substitution into the population inequality proves that L=max(0,q_hat−t_N−a_hat−t_m−η) satisfies Pr(p≥L)≥1−α, conditional on the population error allowance and sampling assumptions. The union bound does not require independence between the two estimation errors, although the stated sampling design supplies independent panels.

review.rationale: The bounded-variable moment inequality applies to independent cluster observations in [0,1]. Markov optimization gives exp(−2nt²), so the selected radii each have tail probability α/2. On their joint event, substituting a lower bound for q and an upper bound for a yields the claimed lower confidence bound. Cross-panel independence is unnecessary for the union-bound step.

argument_steps.title: Separate a sensitivity parameter from a validated guarantee
argument_steps.argument: If η is only a hypothetical sensitivity value, L is only a conditional sensitivity result. If a separate valid procedure supplies an upper confidence bound η_U for c with failure probability at most β, replacing η by η_U yields coverage at least 1−α−β by another union bound, without requiring independence of procedures. A third judge's agreement is not itself such a procedure. With no defensible restriction on c, η=1 is always valid and L=0; the framework then honestly provides no positive reliability certificate. Separate estimation of q and a is one sufficient construction, not a universal requirement: direct truth evaluation or a joint estimator could be preferable when available.

review.rationale: Intersecting the estimator event with a valid event c≤η_U loses at most α+β probability, even with dependence. Setting η=1 makes the bound zero. The step correctly distinguishes hypothetical sensitivity values from validated guarantees and explicitly qualifies separate estimation as sufficient rather than necessary.

argument_steps.title: Specify the discriminating validation test
argument_steps.argument: A proposed implementation test should generate independent task clusters with easy/hard heterogeneity, varying within-task correlation, and a shared judge-error mechanism controlling c. Across repeated panels and several N, m, and r values, compare the frequency L>p against α when the allowance is valid. Include η=0 with perfect reference certification, η=c, a deliberately understated η<c, and perfectly correlated repeated runs. Retain a naive run-independent interval only as a negative control, not as an endorsed method. Ground truth and population probabilities should be known from the finite generative model or derived independently. Such finite tests would check implementation and sensitivity, not prove the coverage theorem or demonstrate real-agent reliability.

review.rationale: The proposed controls distinguish within-task dependence, valid versus understated error allowances, and shared judge errors. Known generative truth permits implementation checks. This is accepted as a discriminating test specification only; it provides no measured coverage or real-agent evidence.

It yields exactly one effect if at least one matching request eventually completes its commit transition. Merely writing the effect and the record separately does not provide this guarantee: explicit crash traces produce either duplicate effects or a false completed record with no effect. These are conditional analytical results and manually derived test expectations, not executed agent experiments.

reasoning_steps.title: Define the state and correctness boundary
reasoning_steps.argument: Let S=(E,D,L,Q,V,J). E is a durable multiset of actual business effects, each containing an effect identifier, operation key k, and full payload p. D is a durable map from k to a completed record (p,result,effect_identifier). L is the agent's durable intent/checkpoint and visible transcript. Q contains pending request and acknowledgment envelopes, each with a distinct delivery identifier. V is volatile service execution state. J is an evaluator-only event journal. For one intended operation (k,p), task correctness requires exactly one effect with that key and payload, and no unintended effect. A completed D entry is an assertion of completion, not the outcome oracle. The evaluator reads E directly and audits its correspondence with D. This intentionally narrow ledger-backed task does not supply an oracle for open-ended agent work.

reasoning_steps.title: Specify failure and observation semantics
reasoning_steps.argument: SEND adds a request (delivery_id,k,p) to Q without changing E or D. DROP permanently removes an envelope before processing; DELAY leaves it eligible for later processing. A service crash discards V but preserves E and D; it does not implicitly cancel network envelopes. Agent restore changes L to its checkpoint but cannot change E,D, or Q. Acknowledgments are separately enqueued and delivered or dropped. Every transition is recorded in J. The agent observes only its configured projection: L, delivered tool messages, and a controlled logical clock. It cannot inspect E,D,Q,J or hidden service metadata in the local-only arm. This restriction must be enforced and audited in an implementation; it is not an assertion about ordinary deployed tools.

reasoning_steps.title: Define atomic processing and prove its safety invariant
reasoning_steps.argument: An atomic PROCESS(k,p) transition behaves as follows. If D[k] is absent, it simultaneously appends one effect e=(id,k,p) to E and installs D[k]=(p,result,id). If D[k] contains the same full payload, it returns the recorded result without changing E or D. If the payload differs, it rejects without an effect. A crash during the atomic transition exposes either its entire before-state or its entire after-state. Starting with E=D=empty, the invariant is: for each key, either D is absent and no effect exists, or D identifies exactly one matching effect and no other effect exists for that key. Induction proves it: an absent-key transition creates precisely the matching pair; replay and rejection preserve it; SEND, DROP, DELAY, acknowledgment handling, and crashes do not alter the pair. Atomic serialization covers simultaneous requests, so both cannot observe an absent key at their commit points. Thus any finite sequence, including delayed duplicate deliveries, preserves at-most-one effect.

reasoning_steps.title: Separate safety, eventual effect, and verified completion
reasoning_steps.argument: The invariant does not imply that an effect ever occurs: all requests might be dropped, or execution might stop before processing. If at least one matching request completes PROCESS, its absent-key branch creates one effect or its replay branch witnesses an existing matching effect. Combining this existence argument with at-most-one gives exactly one effect. An acknowledgment need not reach the agent, so actual correctness does not imply verified completion. Conversely, a finite-time observation of one effect need not establish stable success when a non-deduplicated request remains pending. Final audits must drain all accepted requests under a declared schedule or establish that they have been irrevocably fenced; a timeout alone is not such a fence.

reasoning_steps.title: Manually derive the ordinary-operation ambiguity controls
reasoning_steps.argument: Write a summary state as (N,d,q), where N counts intended-key effects, d=1 means a completed D entry exists, and q counts outstanding requests; omitted acknowledgments are stated separately. In ordinary mode, processing always appends an effect and leaves D empty. T0, no fault: SEND; PROCESS; deliver acknowledgment gives (1,0,0) and visible success. T1, pre-commit loss: SEND; DROP; timeout gives (0,0,0). T2, post-commit acknowledgment loss: SEND; PROCESS; DROP acknowledgment; timeout gives (1,0,0). Restore the same intent checkpoint and expose the same logical-time timeout transcript in T1 and T2. Their agent projections must then be byte-for-byte equal despite different E. Skipping leaves effect counts 0 and 1 respectively; issuing one successfully processed retry leaves counts 1 and 2. This reproduces the relevant ambiguity without assuming an implemented harness already hides every side channel.

reasoning_steps.title: Manually derive atomic recovery and crash traces
reasoning_steps.argument: T3, atomic pre-commit loss: SEND; DROP; timeout; restore; SEND same (k,p); PROCESS gives (1,1,0). T4, atomic post-commit acknowledgment loss: SEND; PROCESS; DROP acknowledgment; timeout; restore; retry same (k,p); PROCESS leaves (1,1,0), and the returned effect identifier equals the original identifier. T5, crash immediately before the atomic commit leaves (0,0,0) after the consumed request is lost; retry creates (1,1,0). Crash immediately after commit but before acknowledgment instead leaves (1,1,0); retry preserves it. The required checks are the full payload, effect identifier, record-effect correspondence, and invariant after every transition, not merely the final count. These are consequences of the atomic model, not evidence that a specific service implements it.

reasoning_steps.title: Give counterexample traces for separately written completed records
reasoning_steps.argument: Consider a deliberately unsafe handler that checks D and, if absent, performs two durable writes without a recovery protocol. T6, effect first: append effect gives (1,0,0); crash before writing D; retry sees no record and appends another effect, then writes D, giving (2,1,0). T7, record first: write a completed record containing a reserved effect identifier, giving (0,1,0); crash before creating that effect; retry treats D as completed and returns success without an effect, leaving (0,1,0). T6 violates at-most-one; T7 violates completed-record soundness and exactly-one. Both failures occur with stable key and payload. These traces refute sufficiency of this naive two-write handler, not all non-atomic implementations: a pending-state protocol with durable recovery, fencing, or downstream deduplication requires separate analysis.

reasoning_steps.title: Expose the delayed-request hazard and the limit of lookup
reasoning_steps.argument: T8: SEND request a; DELAY a; timeout gives (0,0,1). An authoritative lookup now correctly reports no effect. SEND retry b; process b gives (1,0,1); process delayed a gives (2,0,0) in ordinary mode. Thus even a correct lookup of current state is not sufficient to justify a non-idempotent retry when earlier requests remain live. In atomic mode with the same key and payload, the corresponding suffix is (1,1,1) then (1,1,0), because a becomes a replay. Skipping after the timeout also need not mean permanent failure: releasing a can eventually produce one effect. Consequently delayed and dropped requests must be distinct experimental strata. The earlier forced skip-or-one-retry bound must not be transferred unchanged to lookup or pending-request policies.

reasoning_steps.title: Specify negative controls that test the repair assumptions
reasoning_steps.argument: T9, identity drift: after an atomic commit and lost acknowledgment, retry using a fresh key k2; both keys are absent on their first commits, so two effects occur for the same user intention even though per-key invariants hold. T10, payload drift: retry the original key with p2 different from p; the specified atomic handler rejects and leaves E unchanged. T11, retention failure: commit, delete D[k] while retaining E, then retry; the absent-key branch produces a second effect. T12, concurrency: queue two identical requests before processing either; the atomic model yields one effect regardless of their order. A split implementation that lets both workers read absent before either writes can create two. These controls distinguish per-key service correctness from operation-identity preservation, retention, and concurrent orchestration.

reasoning_steps.title: State what the specification advances and what it does not
reasoning_steps.argument: The suite connects initiating faults to propagation and user-visible consequences: lost acknowledgments lead to ambiguous retries, local restore leaves external effects intact, split writes create inconsistent evidence, and live delayed requests can invalidate a recovery decision. It supplies auditable expected traces for the harness and service-property obligations recorded in the supplied extract of artifact 984e8fd3-f76b-46fb-b868-378c2f103425. It does not resolve those empirical obligations, show that real agents preserve keys, or demonstrate causal deployment benefit. Only the incomplete supplied extract was available; its original, one omitted finding, and eleven omitted historical obligations were not inspected. Standard state-machine and fault-injection reasoning is used; material novelty and empirical generality are not assessed.

reasoning_steps.title: Define the state and correctness boundary
reasoning_steps.argument: Let S=(E,D,L,Q,V,J). E is a durable multiset of actual business effects, each containing an effect identifier, operation key k, and full payload p. D is a durable map from k to a completed record (p,result,effect_identifier). L is the agent's durable intent/checkpoint and visible transcript. Q contains pending request and acknowledgment envelopes, each with a distinct delivery identifier. V is volatile service execution state. J is an evaluator-only event journal. For one intended operation (k,p), task correctness requires exactly one effect with that key and payload, and no unintended effect. A completed D entry is an assertion of completion, not the outcome oracle. The evaluator reads E directly and audits its correspondence with D. This intentionally narrow ledger-backed task does not supply an oracle for open-ended agent work.

review.rationale: This defines a coherent conditional ledger-backed model. Distinguishing actual E from assertions in D prevents the completion record from becoming its own correctness oracle.

reasoning_steps.title: Specify failure and observation semantics
reasoning_steps.argument: SEND adds a request (delivery_id,k,p) to Q without changing E or D. DROP permanently removes an envelope before processing; DELAY leaves it eligible for later processing. A service crash discards V but preserves E and D; it does not implicitly cancel network envelopes. Agent restore changes L to its checkpoint but cannot change E,D, or Q. Acknowledgments are separately enqueued and delivered or dropped. Every transition is recorded in J. The agent observes only its configured projection: L, delivered tool messages, and a controlled logical clock. It cannot inspect E,D,Q,J or hidden service metadata in the local-only arm. This restriction must be enforced and audited in an implementation; it is not an assertion about ordinary deployed tools.

review.rationale: The stated premises consistently distinguish permanent drop from delay, preserve external durable state across local restoration, and restrict agent observations. They are model definitions, not established deployment properties.

reasoning_steps.title: Define atomic processing and prove its safety invariant
reasoning_steps.argument: An atomic PROCESS(k,p) transition behaves as follows. If D[k] is absent, it simultaneously appends one effect e=(id,k,p) to E and installs D[k]=(p,result,id). If D[k] contains the same full payload, it returns the recorded result without changing E or D. If the payload differs, it rejects without an effect. A crash during the atomic transition exposes either its entire before-state or its entire after-state. Starting with E=D=empty, the invariant is: for each key, either D is absent and no effect exists, or D identifies exactly one matching effect and no other effect exists for that key. Induction proves it: an absent-key transition creates precisely the matching pair; replay and rejection preserve it; SEND, DROP, DELAY, acknowledgment handling, and crashes do not alter the pair. Atomic serialization covers simultaneous requests, so both cannot observe an absent key at their commit points. Thus any finite sequence, including delayed duplicate deliveries, preserves at-most-one effect.

review.rationale: Starting from empty E and D, each permitted durable-state transition preserves the claimed correspondence. Serialization prevents two absent-key commits, and all other listed transitions leave the pair unchanged. This establishes per-key safety only under the stated atomicity and retention premises.

reasoning_steps.title: Separate safety, eventual effect, and verified completion
reasoning_steps.argument: The invariant does not imply that an effect ever occurs: all requests might be dropped, or execution might stop before processing. If at least one matching request completes PROCESS, its absent-key branch creates one effect or its replay branch witnesses an existing matching effect. Combining this existence argument with at-most-one gives exactly one effect. An acknowledgment need not reach the agent, so actual correctness does not imply verified completion. Conversely, a finite-time observation of one effect need not establish stable success when a non-deduplicated request remains pending. Final audits must drain all accepted requests under a declared schedule or establish that they have been irrevocably fenced; a timeout alone is not such a fence.

review.rationale: With the stable matching key and payload, a completed PROCESS either creates the effect or observes its existing matching record. Combining existence with the invariant gives exactly one. Lost acknowledgments and live ordinary requests correctly separate actual correctness, agent knowledge, and stable finality.

reasoning_steps.title: Manually derive the ordinary-operation ambiguity controls
reasoning_steps.argument: Write a summary state as (N,d,q), where N counts intended-key effects, d=1 means a completed D entry exists, and q counts outstanding requests; omitted acknowledgments are stated separately. In ordinary mode, processing always appends an effect and leaves D empty. T0, no fault: SEND; PROCESS; deliver acknowledgment gives (1,0,0) and visible success. T1, pre-commit loss: SEND; DROP; timeout gives (0,0,0). T2, post-commit acknowledgment loss: SEND; PROCESS; DROP acknowledgment; timeout gives (1,0,0). Restore the same intent checkpoint and expose the same logical-time timeout transcript in T1 and T2. Their agent projections must then be byte-for-byte equal despite different E. Skipping leaves effect counts 0 and 1 respectively; issuing one successfully processed retry leaves counts 1 and 2. This reproduces the relevant ambiguity without assuming an implemented harness already hides every side channel.

review.rationale: The completed ordinary-operation traces yield effect counts zero and one at the timeout, and one and two after a successful retry. Equal restored checkpoints and controlled timeout transcripts give equal projections in this stipulated local-only model; implementation equality remains untested.

reasoning_steps.title: Manually derive atomic recovery and crash traces
reasoning_steps.argument: T3, atomic pre-commit loss: SEND; DROP; timeout; restore; SEND same (k,p); PROCESS gives (1,1,0). T4, atomic post-commit acknowledgment loss: SEND; PROCESS; DROP acknowledgment; timeout; restore; retry same (k,p); PROCESS leaves (1,1,0), and the returned effect identifier equals the original identifier. T5, crash immediately before the atomic commit leaves (0,0,0) after the consumed request is lost; retry creates (1,1,0). Crash immediately after commit but before acknowledgment instead leaves (1,1,0); retry preserves it. The required checks are the full payload, effect identifier, record-effect correspondence, and invariant after every transition, not merely the final count. These are consequences of the atomic model, not evidence that a specific service implements it.

review.rationale: T3/T4 and the durable-state outcomes around atomic commitment follow from the handler. T5 additionally relies on an unstated request-consumption transition.
review.objection: Specify when the delivery leaves Q and enters V. Without that rule, a crash immediately before PROCESS does not determine whether q is zero or one, or whether subsequent redelivery is possible. This does not invalidate the E/D safety invariant.

reasoning_steps.title: Give counterexample traces for separately written completed records
reasoning_steps.argument: Consider a deliberately unsafe handler that checks D and, if absent, performs two durable writes without a recovery protocol. T6, effect first: append effect gives (1,0,0); crash before writing D; retry sees no record and appends another effect, then writes D, giving (2,1,0). T7, record first: write a completed record containing a reserved effect identifier, giving (0,1,0); crash before creating that effect; retry treats D as completed and returns success without an effect, leaving (0,1,0). T6 violates at-most-one; T7 violates completed-record soundness and exactly-one. Both failures occur with stable key and payload. These traces refute sufficiency of this naive two-write handler, not all non-atomic implementations: a pending-state protocol with durable recovery, fencing, or downstream deduplication requires separate analysis.

review.rationale: For these explicitly naive handlers, effect-first leaves a durable effect without a record, enabling a second effect; record-first leaves a completed record without its effect, causing a false replay success. The restriction to these handlers avoids an unsupported impossibility claim about all split-write protocols.

reasoning_steps.title: Expose the delayed-request hazard and the limit of lookup
reasoning_steps.argument: T8: SEND request a; DELAY a; timeout gives (0,0,1). An authoritative lookup now correctly reports no effect. SEND retry b; process b gives (1,0,1); process delayed a gives (2,0,0) in ordinary mode. Thus even a correct lookup of current state is not sufficient to justify a non-idempotent retry when earlier requests remain live. In atomic mode with the same key and payload, the corresponding suffix is (1,1,1) then (1,1,0), because a becomes a replay. Skipping after the timeout also need not mean permanent failure: releasing a can eventually produce one effect. Consequently delayed and dropped requests must be distinct experimental strata. The earlier forced skip-or-one-retry bound must not be transferred unchanged to lookup or pending-request policies.

review.rationale: An unprocessed delayed request can remain live after a truthful lookup. Processing the retry and then that request creates two ordinary effects, whereas stable-key atomic processing makes the latter a replay. The trace establishes lookup insufficiency without fencing, not impossibility for stronger lookup protocols.

reasoning_steps.title: Specify negative controls that test the repair assumptions
reasoning_steps.argument: T9, identity drift: after an atomic commit and lost acknowledgment, retry using a fresh key k2; both keys are absent on their first commits, so two effects occur for the same user intention even though per-key invariants hold. T10, payload drift: retry the original key with p2 different from p; the specified atomic handler rejects and leaves E unchanged. T11, retention failure: commit, delete D[k] while retaining E, then retry; the absent-key branch produces a second effect. T12, concurrency: queue two identical requests before processing either; the atomic model yields one effect regardless of their order. A split implementation that lets both workers read absent before either writes can create two. These controls distinguish per-key service correctness from operation-identity preservation, retention, and concurrent orchestration.

review.rationale: Fresh keys evade per-key protection, payload mismatch is rejected by definition, deleting D breaks the invariant's retention premise, and serialized identical requests create one effect in either order. These controls isolate assumptions rather than contradict the positive theorem.

reasoning_steps.argument: The suite connects initiating faults to propagation and user-visible consequences: lost acknowledgments lead to ambiguous retries, local restore leaves external effects intact, split writes create inconsistent evidence, and live delayed requests can invalidate a recovery decision. Only the incomplete supplied extract was available; its original, one omitted finding, and eleven omitted historical obligations were not inspected. Standard state-machine and fault-injection reasoning is used; material novelty and empirical generality are not assessed.

argument_steps.title: Give counterexample traces for separately written completed records
argument_steps.argument: Consider a deliberately unsafe handler that checks D and, if absent, performs two durable writes without a recovery protocol. T6, effect first: append effect gives (1,0,0); crash before writing D; retry sees no record and appends another effect, then writes D, giving (2,1,0). T7, record first: write a completed record containing a reserved effect identifier, giving (0,1,0); crash before creating that effect; retry treats D as completed and returns success without an effect, leaving (0,1,0). T6 violates at-most-one; T7 violates completed-record soundness and exactly-one. Both failures occur with stable key and payload. These traces refute sufficiency of this naive two-write handler, not all non-atomic implementations: a pending-state protocol with durable recovery, fencing, or downstream deduplication requires separate analysis.

review.rationale: For these explicitly naive handlers, effect-first leaves a durable effect without a record, enabling a second effect; record-first leaves a completed record without its effect, causing a false replay success. The restriction to these handlers avoids an unsupported impossibility claim about all split-write protocols.

argument_steps.title: Expose the delayed-request hazard and the limit of lookup
argument_steps.argument: T8: SEND request a; DELAY a; timeout gives (0,0,1). An authoritative lookup now correctly reports no effect. SEND retry b; process b gives (1,0,1); process delayed a gives (2,0,0) in ordinary mode. Thus even a correct lookup of current state is not sufficient to justify a non-idempotent retry when earlier requests remain live. In atomic mode with the same key and payload, the corresponding suffix is (1,1,1) then (1,1,0), because a becomes a replay. Skipping after the timeout also need not mean permanent failure: releasing a can eventually produce one effect. Consequently delayed and dropped requests must be distinct experimental strata. The earlier forced skip-or-one-retry bound must not be transferred unchanged to lookup or pending-request policies.

review.rationale: An unprocessed delayed request can remain live after a truthful lookup. Processing the retry and then that request creates two ordinary effects, whereas stable-key atomic processing makes the latter a replay. The trace establishes lookup insufficiency without fencing, not impossibility for stronger lookup protocols.

argument_steps.title: Specify negative controls that test the repair assumptions
argument_steps.argument: T9, identity drift: after an atomic commit and lost acknowledgment, retry using a fresh key k2; both keys are absent on their first commits, so two effects occur for the same user intention even though per-key invariants hold. T10, payload drift: retry the original key with p2 different from p; the specified atomic handler rejects and leaves E unchanged. T11, retention failure: commit, delete D[k] while retaining E, then retry; the absent-key branch produces a second effect. T12, concurrency: queue two identical requests before processing either; the atomic model yields one effect regardless of their order. A split implementation that lets both workers read absent before either writes can create two. These controls distinguish per-key service correctness from operation-identity preservation, retention, and concurrent orchestration.

review.rationale: Fresh keys evade per-key protection, payload mismatch is rejected by definition, deleting D breaks the invariant's retention premise, and serialized identical requests create one effect in either order. These controls isolate assumptions rather than contradict the positive theorem.

reasoning_steps.argument: The supplied extract of artifact 984e8fd3-f76b-46fb-b868-378c2f103425 describes indistinguishable pre-commit loss and post-commit acknowledgment loss, and identifies service atomicity and harness observability as unresolved. Its original artifact is not available here; assumptions, evidence status, and other fields are truncated, and one additional finding is omitted.
