I leave its empirical and broader workflow claims unresolved and independently define the narrower model below.

reasoning_steps.title: Define the state and observation boundary
reasoning_steps.argument: One intended business operation has key k and exact canonical payload p. Durable business state E is an append-only collection of effect entries; N is the number attributable to this intended operation, including erroneous retries under another key. Durable service map D stores k -> (p, effect identifier, result). Durable agent checkpoint C stores the intended k and p. Network state Q contains pending requests and responses. Volatile service state V contains incomplete handlers. Evaluator-only log L records delivery, commit, crash, and response events. The agent observes only C and its tool-visible transcript O, not E, D, Q, V, or L. Attribution metadata used by the evaluator is not an extra service deduplication mechanism. Correctness is N=1; receipt of a success response is a separate observable.

reasoning_steps.title: Specify delivery, ordinary execution, and crash transitions
reasoning_steps.argument: Send adds a request to Q. Drop permanently removes it before execution; delay leaves it in Q and permits later delivery. A timeout changes O but neither cancels Q nor establishes that execution failed. The ordinary service appends one effect for each delivered valid request and then enqueues a response. Dropping a response does not undo an effect. A service crash clears V but preserves E and D; it does not implicitly cancel network requests. An agent restart restores C and the specified checkpoint-visible transcript. At the audit horizon, pending requests must be reported; final effect correctness is assessed after draining the finite test schedule or establishing a real cancellation barrier, not merely after an agent timeout.

reasoning_steps.title: Specify the atomic deduplicating alternative
reasoning_steps.argument: For a delivered request (k,p), the atomic service performs one serializable durable transition. If k is absent, it appends one effect and installs D[k]=(p,id,result) together. If k is present with identical p, it changes neither E nor D and returns the stored result. If k is present with different p, it rejects without an effect. Concurrent handlers for the same key are serialized at this transition. A crash can leave either the complete pre-transition state or the complete post-transition state, never one write alone. A response is generated only after the durable transition. No records expire during the retry and delayed-delivery horizon. This specifies a transactional boundary around the actual business effect, not just a local record describing a separate external action.

reasoning_steps.title: Derive safety and separate it from progress
reasoning_steps.argument: Initially E and D are empty for k. Inductively, a first atomic insertion creates exactly one effect paired with one matching record. Every later matching request is read-only; mismatching requests reject; drops, timeouts, and crashes cannot change the durable pair. Thus D[k] exists if and only if exactly one corresponding effect exists, and that effect matches its stored payload and identifier. Therefore N<=1 for the intended operation if every attempt preserves its unique k and p. If at least one valid request eventually completes the atomic transition, the absent-key branch creates an effect or the present-key branch witnesses an existing one, so N=1. Without that delivery/commit premise, perpetual dropping leaves N=0. Even with N=1, the agent need not know completion if every response is lost.

reasoning_steps.title: Derive baseline traces and distinguish delay from loss
reasoning_steps.argument: Each trace starts fresh at N=0. T1, ordinary no fault: deliver original, append, deliver acknowledgment -> N=1. T2, ordinary pre-commit drop: drop original, timeout, deliver retry -> N=1. T3, ordinary lost acknowledgment: deliver original and append, drop acknowledgment, timeout, deliver retry -> N=2. T4, ordinary delayed original: hold original, timeout, deliver retry and append, then release original and append -> N=2. Restoring the same local checkpoint changes none of these counts. T2 and T3 can have exactly the same agent-visible recovery prefix by construction despite different external states. T4 shows why treating all timeouts as permanent drops would invalidate the test.

reasoning_steps.title: Derive atomic-service traces, including crash boundaries
reasoning_steps.argument: Write states as (N, number of records for k). T5, atomic pre-commit drop followed by delivered retry: (0,0)->(1,1). T6, atomic original commit with lost acknowledgment followed by matching retry: (0,0)->(1,1)->(1,1). T7, delayed original released after the matching retry, or two concurrent matching deliveries: serialization gives (0,0)->(1,1)->(1,1), regardless of delivery order. T8, crash at the atomic transition: the recovered state is either (0,0) or (1,1); a subsequently delivered matching retry ends at (1,1) in either case. The mixed states (1,0) and (0,1) are forbidden observations for this implementation. Acknowledgment loss affects knowledge, not these durable counts.

reasoning_steps.title: Construct counterexamples to separately written key tables
reasoning_steps.argument: T9, effect-first implementation: append effect -> (1,0), crash before writing the key record, recover, retry sees no record and appends again, then writes the record -> (2,1). T10, record-first implementation with a record treated as completed: install record -> (0,1), crash before effect, recover, retry returns the cached completion and performs no effect -> (0,1). These are counterexamples to those two explicitly defined naive implementations, not to all non-atomic protocols. A pending-record protocol with reconciliation has different transitions and needs a separate proof; labeling a record 'pending' alone does not establish that proof.

reasoning_steps.title: Specify assumption-breaking controls
reasoning_steps.argument: T11, after an atomic success retry with the same k but a different payload: rejection must leave (1,1), and the mismatch must be observable to the agent. T12, retry the same intended operation with a new key: the service legitimately inserts another record and effect, so total N=2; this tests agent identity preservation, not a violation of per-key atomicity. T13, delete the original record after success while retaining its effect, then deliver a matching retry: a fresh insertion produces N=2. This demonstrates the retention requirement. Also reuse a key for two genuinely distinct intended operations: the second may be suppressed or rejected, showing why uniqueness across operations matters. These controls make scope violations visible instead of counting them as unexplained regressions.

reasoning_steps.title: Define the audit contract and causal comparison
reasoning_steps.argument: For every trace, retain full evaluator event order, durable snapshots at each crash boundary, final effect-to-intent attribution, request key/payload lineage, response content, pending requests, and the exact actor-visible recovery prefix. The H0/H1 indistinguishability assertion requires equality of every actor-accessible field before the recovery decision, including timing, tool metadata, restored memory, and status channels; evaluator-only differences are allowed. Begin with scripted identical retry behavior to isolate service semantics, then hold service semantics fixed while testing whether real agents preserve identity across restart and replanning. Use no-fault runs to expose overhead and regressions. Report all-run verified success, duplicate/missing effects, false completion, unresolved outcomes, latency, tool use, and cost separately. Scripted trace agreement validates only those traces; repeated agent trials and held-out workflows are still required for an architectural benefit claim.

reasoning_assessments.rationale: The supplied extract does identify ambiguous commitment and unresolved observability and atomicity. The step uses it only to motivate a test and explicitly declines to import missing premises or empirical support.

As a premise of the explicitly conditional model, the separation of effects, records, checkpoints, network state, and evaluator logs is coherent. Counting effects by intended operation rather than key correctly allows detection of identity-changing retries.

These stipulated transitions consistently distinguish permanent loss from still-deliverable requests. A timeout changes knowledge rather than external state, and draining the finite schedule or establishing cancellation prevents premature final auditing.

The atomic alternative is a valid conditional premise: serialization excludes concurrent absent-key insertions, crash atomicity excludes mixed durable states, and retention preserves replay recognition. It explicitly includes the actual effect rather than an uncoordinated downstream action.

From an empty per-key state, the only effect-creating transition installs exactly one matching record. Replays, mismatches, and modeled faults cannot add another effect. Stable unique identity transfers this per-key invariant to the intended operation. Eventual valid commitment establishes existence; response delivery is not needed for effect existence.

Counting one append per delivered ordinary request gives the stated terminal counts 1, 1, 2, and 2. Matching timeout prefixes for T2 and T3 are possible under the observation model, but remain a harness construction requirement rather than an observed fact.

The atomic transition permits only the empty or paired durable state at a crash. A subsequent matching delivery produces or reuses the pair. Serialization gives the same result for delayed and concurrent matching requests, so the listed traces follow from the premises.

Effect-first recovery repeats the effect because the record is absent; completed-record-first recovery suppresses the effect because completion is falsely represented. The resulting states are correctly derived, and the conclusion is properly restricted to those handlers.

Mismatch rejection leaves the existing pair unchanged. A new key or deletion of the retained record permits a fresh insertion, while cross-operation key reuse can suppress legitimate work. These are valid assumption-breaking controls, not violations of the conditional theorem.

The proposed logs and snapshots cover the stated invariant and observation boundary, and separating scripted service tests from agent identity tests improves attribution. The step explicitly limits trace agreement and does not infer measured causal benefit.

reasoning_steps.title: Define the state and observation boundary
reasoning_steps.argument: One intended business operation has key k and exact canonical payload p. Durable business state E is an append-only collection of effect entries; N is the number attributable to this intended operation, including erroneous retries under another key. Durable service map D stores k -> (p, effect identifier, result). Durable agent checkpoint C stores the intended k and p. Network state Q contains pending requests and responses. Volatile service state V contains incomplete handlers. Evaluator-only log L records delivery, commit, crash, and response events. The agent observes only C and its tool-visible transcript O, not E, D, Q, V, or L. Attribution metadata used by the evaluator is not an extra service deduplication mechanism. Correctness is N=1; receipt of a success response is a separate observable.

review.rationale: As a premise of the explicitly conditional model, the separation of effects, records, checkpoints, network state, and evaluator logs is coherent. Counting effects by intended operation rather than key correctly allows detection of identity-changing retries.

reasoning_steps.title: Specify delivery, ordinary execution, and crash transitions
reasoning_steps.argument: Send adds a request to Q. Drop permanently removes it before execution; delay leaves it in Q and permits later delivery. A timeout changes O but neither cancels Q nor establishes that execution failed. The ordinary service appends one effect for each delivered valid request and then enqueues a response. Dropping a response does not undo an effect. A service crash clears V but preserves E and D; it does not implicitly cancel network requests. An agent restart restores C and the specified checkpoint-visible transcript. At the audit horizon, pending requests must be reported; final effect correctness is assessed after draining the finite test schedule or establishing a real cancellation barrier, not merely after an agent timeout.

review.rationale: These stipulated transitions consistently distinguish permanent loss from still-deliverable requests. A timeout changes knowledge rather than external state, and draining the finite schedule or establishing cancellation prevents premature final auditing.

reasoning_steps.title: Specify the atomic deduplicating alternative
reasoning_steps.argument: For a delivered request (k,p), the atomic service performs one serializable durable transition. If k is absent, it appends one effect and installs D[k]=(p,id,result) together. If k is present with identical p, it changes neither E nor D and returns the stored result. If k is present with different p, it rejects without an effect. Concurrent handlers for the same key are serialized at this transition. A crash can leave either the complete pre-transition state or the complete post-transition state, never one write alone. A response is generated only after the durable transition. No records expire during the retry and delayed-delivery horizon. This specifies a transactional boundary around the actual business effect, not just a local record describing a separate external action.

review.rationale: The atomic alternative is a valid conditional premise: serialization excludes concurrent absent-key insertions, crash atomicity excludes mixed durable states, and retention preserves replay recognition. It explicitly includes the actual effect rather than an uncoordinated downstream action.

reasoning_steps.title: Derive safety and separate it from progress
reasoning_steps.argument: Initially E and D are empty for k. Inductively, a first atomic insertion creates exactly one effect paired with one matching record. Every later matching request is read-only; mismatching requests reject; drops, timeouts, and crashes cannot change the durable pair. Thus D[k] exists if and only if exactly one corresponding effect exists, and that effect matches its stored payload and identifier. Therefore N<=1 for the intended operation if every attempt preserves its unique k and p. If at least one valid request eventually completes the atomic transition, the absent-key branch creates an effect or the present-key branch witnesses an existing one, so N=1. Without that delivery/commit premise, perpetual dropping leaves N=0. Even with N=1, the agent need not know completion if every response is lost.

review.rationale: From an empty per-key state, the only effect-creating transition installs exactly one matching record. Replays, mismatches, and modeled faults cannot add another effect. Stable unique identity transfers this per-key invariant to the intended operation. Eventual valid commitment establishes existence; response delivery is not needed for effect existence.

reasoning_steps.title: Derive baseline traces and distinguish delay from loss
reasoning_steps.argument: Each trace starts fresh at N=0. T1, ordinary no fault: deliver original, append, deliver acknowledgment -> N=1. T2, ordinary pre-commit drop: drop original, timeout, deliver retry -> N=1. T3, ordinary lost acknowledgment: deliver original and append, drop acknowledgment, timeout, deliver retry -> N=2. T4, ordinary delayed original: hold original, timeout, deliver retry and append, then release original and append -> N=2. Restoring the same local checkpoint changes none of these counts. T2 and T3 can have exactly the same agent-visible recovery prefix by construction despite different external states. T4 shows why treating all timeouts as permanent drops would invalidate the test.

review.rationale: Counting one append per delivered ordinary request gives the stated terminal counts 1, 1, 2, and 2. Matching timeout prefixes for T2 and T3 are possible under the observation model, but remain a harness construction requirement rather than an observed fact.

reasoning_steps.title: Derive atomic-service traces, including crash boundaries
reasoning_steps.argument: Write states as (N, number of records for k). T5, atomic pre-commit drop followed by delivered retry: (0,0)->(1,1). T6, atomic original commit with lost acknowledgment followed by matching retry: (0,0)->(1,1)->(1,1). T7, delayed original released after the matching retry, or two concurrent matching deliveries: serialization gives (0,0)->(1,1)->(1,1), regardless of delivery order. T8, crash at the atomic transition: the recovered state is either (0,0) or (1,1); a subsequently delivered matching retry ends at (1,1) in either case. The mixed states (1,0) and (0,1) are forbidden observations for this implementation. Acknowledgment loss affects knowledge, not these durable counts.

review.rationale: The atomic transition permits only the empty or paired durable state at a crash. A subsequent matching delivery produces or reuses the pair. Serialization gives the same result for delayed and concurrent matching requests, so the listed traces follow from the premises.

reasoning_steps.title: Construct counterexamples to separately written key tables
reasoning_steps.argument: T9, effect-first implementation: append effect -> (1,0), crash before writing the key record, recover, retry sees no record and appends again, then writes the record -> (2,1). T10, record-first implementation with a record treated as completed: install record -> (0,1), crash before effect, recover, retry returns the cached completion and performs no effect -> (0,1). These are counterexamples to those two explicitly defined naive implementations, not to all non-atomic protocols. A pending-record protocol with reconciliation has different transitions and needs a separate proof; labeling a record 'pending' alone does not establish that proof.

review.rationale: Effect-first recovery repeats the effect because the record is absent; completed-record-first recovery suppresses the effect because completion is falsely represented. The resulting states are correctly derived, and the conclusion is properly restricted to those handlers.

reasoning_steps.title: Specify assumption-breaking controls
reasoning_steps.argument: T11, after an atomic success retry with the same k but a different payload: rejection must leave (1,1), and the mismatch must be observable to the agent. T12, retry the same intended operation with a new key: the service legitimately inserts another record and effect, so total N=2; this tests agent identity preservation, not a violation of per-key atomicity. T13, delete the original record after success while retaining its effect, then deliver a matching retry: a fresh insertion produces N=2. This demonstrates the retention requirement. Also reuse a key for two genuinely distinct intended operations: the second may be suppressed or rejected, showing why uniqueness across operations matters. These controls make scope violations visible instead of counting them as unexplained regressions.

review.rationale: Mismatch rejection leaves the existing pair unchanged. A new key or deletion of the retained record permits a fresh insertion, while cross-operation key reuse can suppress legitimate work. These are valid assumption-breaking controls, not violations of the conditional theorem.

reasoning_steps.title: Define the audit contract and causal comparison
reasoning_steps.argument: For every trace, retain full evaluator event order, durable snapshots at each crash boundary, final effect-to-intent attribution, request key/payload lineage, response content, pending requests, and the exact actor-visible recovery prefix. The H0/H1 indistinguishability assertion requires equality of every actor-accessible field before the recovery decision, including timing, tool metadata, restored memory, and status channels; evaluator-only differences are allowed. Begin with scripted identical retry behavior to isolate service semantics, then hold service semantics fixed while testing whether real agents preserve identity across restart and replanning. Use no-fault runs to expose overhead and regressions. Report all-run verified success, duplicate/missing effects, false completion, unresolved outcomes, latency, tool use, and cost separately. Scripted trace agreement validates only those traces; repeated agent trials and held-out workflows are still required for an architectural benefit claim.

review.rationale: The proposed logs and snapshots cover the stated invariant and observation boundary, and separating scripted service tests from agent identity tests improves attribution. The step explicitly limits trace agreement and does not infer measured causal benefit.

artifacts.strategy_title: Understand failure propagation and recovery in autonomous AI agents
artifacts.claim_or_question: Under the explicit destructive-dequeue lifecycle defined here, RECEIVE removes a request delivery from Q and places it only in volatile V. A pre-commit service crash therefore loses that consumed delivery; it does not redeliver it. Requests still in Q survive the service crash. Conditional on serialized, crash-durable atomic effect/deduplication updates, the refined T5, T8, and both T12 orders preserve the durable E/D invariant. This closes the identified specification gap, not an implementation or experimental evidence gap.
artifacts.method: Refine only the request lifecycle and manually evaluate the affected traces from empty durable state. The specification hypothesis is that explicitly separating dequeue, durable processing, and acknowledgment enqueue makes every request's fate determinate without changing the atomic E/D safety argument. The discriminating checks are delivery-ID conservation, exact pending and terminal request locations, and effect-record correspondence after every event. T8 includes an ordinary non-deduplicated control. These are manual deductions, not executed experiments. The relevant earlier timeout and interrupted review are operational limitations, not counterexamples; no unavailable runtime is requested. The supplied peer extracts 0310e2ff-4aa0-4c95-b1a8-795559e484b8 and faca8cd0-991f-46a4-91d4-288bb0cd53ea do not change this lifecycle choice: judge validity and actual service atomicity remain unverified, and no peer result is adopted as an independently established premise.
assumptions: The modeled operation is ledger-backed, and all its effects occur through the defined PROCESS transition; E and D initially are empty.

RECEIVE is destructive dequeue into volatile execution state, with no retained broker lease or automatic redelivery. The independent envelope pool Q survives service crashes; explicit network drops remain possible.

Atomic mode serializes the current-D test, effect creation, and completed-record write in one crash-durable transition. Records are retained, operation keys do not collide, and all retries in these traces preserve the same full payload and key.

PROCESS and ACK_ENQUEUE are distinct abstract transitions; ACK_ENQUEUE atomically transfers a processed worker into one pending acknowledgment. Crashes preserve durable E/D and Q but erase all workers.
The manual traces use exactly the displayed schedules. They establish no fairness or eventual-processing property for arbitrary executions.

No computation, implementation, service audit, agent trial, literature inspection, or external verification occurred. artifacts.skeptic_response:
The requested lifecycle refinement is complete within its explicit model. RECEIVE destructively transfers a delivery from Q_R to volatile V; CRASH loses consumed workers without reconstructing their deliveries, while preserving envelopes still in Q. PROCESS and ACK_ENQUEUE are distinct, so the two T5 crash boundaries now have determinate request and reply outcomes. I checked the T5, T8, and both T12 tables: request locations, terminal records, acknowledgment locations, and durable E/D states are consistent after each displayed event. The three recorded lifecycle objections are addressed at the specification level only.

The cycle-1 safety argument and split-write counterexamples in artifact 4435b6ec-fefc-43a1-8706-a3a6794dbbe5 remain supported under their original assumptions; no rewrite is needed. The current refinement strengthens reproducibility of the proposed test specification, not evidence of deployed reliability. No computation, implementation audit, or agent trial occurred. Avoiding another unavailable execution request is appropriate operational recovery, not empirical progress. This is a useful completed local conclusion; the broader project remains partial, with empirical and historical duties preserved.

investigator_output.claim: Under the explicit destructive-dequeue lifecycle defined here, RECEIVE removes a request delivery from Q and places it only in volatile V. A pre-commit service crash therefore loses that consumed delivery; it does not redeliver it. Requests still in Q survive the service crash. Conditional on serialized, crash-durable atomic effect/deduplication updates, the refined T5, T8, and both T12 orders preserve the durable E/D invariant. This closes the identified specification gap, not an implementation or experimental evidence gap.
investigator_output.method: Refine only the request lifecycle and manually evaluate the affected traces from empty durable state. The specification hypothesis is that explicitly separating dequeue, durable processing, and acknowledgment enqueue makes every request's fate determinate without changing the atomic E/D safety argument. The discriminating checks are delivery-ID conservation, exact pending and terminal request locations, and effect-record correspondence after every event. T8 includes an ordinary non-deduplicated control. These are manual deductions, not executed experiments. reasoning_steps.title: State, identifiers, and table notation
reasoning_steps.argument: Retain S=(E,D,L,Q,V,J) from the supplied extract of artifact 4435b6ec-fefc-43a1-8706-a3a6794dbbe5. E is the durable effect multiset; D is the durable completed-record map; L is agent state; J is evaluator-only event history. Partition Q into request envelopes Q_R and acknowledgment envelopes Q_A. A request is (x,k,p), where delivery ID x is globally fresh, independently of stable operation key k. An acknowledgment has a fresh envelope ID alpha_x, correlation field x, and the processing outcome. Retries use a new delivery ID but the same k,p. Q is an independently maintained network-envelope pool: it survives service crashes but permits explicit DROP. It is not a durable broker with automatic redelivery. V contains a service up/down flag and volatile workers xR=(x,k,p,ready) or xC=(x,k,p,processed,outcome). Multiple workers are allowed. Tables display worker entries only; CRASH makes the service down and RESTART makes it up. '-' means empty. T is an evaluator-only terminal-request map derived from J, not additional recoverable service state: L0=lost before processing, L1=processed but reply lost before enqueue, F=handler finished with acknowledgment enqueued, X=explicitly dropped from Q_R. Each trace starts with empty E,D,Q,V,T and an up service.

reasoning_steps.title: SEND, RECEIVE, delay, and drop
reasoning_steps.argument: SEND(x,k,p) adds exactly one fresh request envelope x to Q_R. RECEIVE(x) requires an up service and an eligible x in Q_R; it atomically removes x from Q_R and installs xR in V. RECEIVE changes neither E nor D and creates no acknowledgment. No copy or lease for x remains in Q. DELAY(x) makes no location change and merely withholds its RECEIVE until release. DROP(x) removes x from Q_R and records T[x]=X; dropping an acknowledgment instead removes its envelope from Q_A and records that acknowledgment's loss in J. A timeout does not remove an envelope or worker. Agent restore changes L only. There is no implicit duplicate delivery: an explicit retry is a new SEND with a fresh delivery ID.

reasoning_steps.title: PROCESS is separate from acknowledgment enqueue
reasoning_steps.argument: PROCESS(x) requires xR and an up service. In atomic mode, it tests current D at the serialized processing point, not at RECEIVE. If D[k] is absent, it atomically appends e=(effect_id,k,p) to E and installs D[k]=(p,result,effect_id). If D[k] matches p, it leaves E,D unchanged and obtains the recorded result and effect ID. If the payload differs, it leaves E,D unchanged and obtains a mismatch rejection. The transition replaces xR with xC carrying that outcome; x remains absent from Q_R. ACK_ENQUEUE(x) requires xC, inserts alpha_x into Q_A, removes xC from V, and records T[x]=F. This enqueue/removal is one abstract transition, so it cannot emit two acknowledgments for one worker. ACK_DELIVER(alpha_x) removes that envelope from Q_A, appends its correlated response to L, and records delivery in J. It does not change T[x], E, or D. For the ordinary control, PROCESS always appends a fresh effect and leaves D empty, then creates xC in the same way.

reasoning_steps.title: Crash boundary and request accounting
reasoning_steps.argument: CRASH clears every worker from V and sets the service down. For each xR it records T[x]=L0; for each xC it records T[x]=L1. It preserves E,D,Q_R,Q_A,L and prior terminal records. RESTART sets the service up with no workers; it reconstructs no consumed delivery. Thus a crash before RECEIVE leaves x queued, a crash after RECEIVE but before PROCESS loses x without an effect, a crash after PROCESS but before ACK_ENQUEUE loses only the volatile reply, and a crash after ACK_ENQUEUE leaves alpha_x pending in Q_A. A crash concurrent with atomic PROCESS is represented by either its before-state followed by CRASH or its complete after-state followed by CRASH; a partial E/D write is excluded by premise. The sent request IDs partition disjointly into Q_R, worker IDs in V, and terminal IDs in T. SEND introduces one ID, RECEIVE transfers it, PROCESS changes its worker phase, and enqueue/drop/crash transfers it to T. This proves complete request accounting inductively. Ack IDs similarly partition into Q_A and the delivered/dropped acknowledgment events in J. No automatic redelivery occurs after a pre-commit crash in this model; durable lease/redelivery semantics would be a different model.

reasoning_steps.title: Durable invariant and ledger abbreviations
reasoning_steps.argument: For each key, invariant I is: either D[k] is absent and E contains no effect for k, or D[k]=(p,r,id) and E contains exactly one effect for k, namely (id,k,p), whose recorded result is r. Define Z=(E=empty,D=empty). Define P_x=(E={e_x},D[k]=(p,r_x,id_x)), with e_x=(id_x,k,p) created by delivery x. Define O_b=(E={e_b},D=empty) and O_ba=(E={e_b,e_a},D=empty) for the ordinary control. Z and every P_x satisfy I, including full payload and identifier correspondence, not just counts. O_b and O_ba fail I because ordinary mode intentionally has no D record; O_b still has at-most-one effect, whereas O_ba does not. In atomic mode, first PROCESS creates one matching pair, replay/rejection preserve it, and every other lifecycle transition leaves E,D unchanged. This proves I from empty initialization despite crashes and concurrent workers. It supplies safety only: loss of every ready worker can leave Z forever.

reasoning_steps.title: T5: consumed request lost immediately before commit
reasoning_steps.argument:
All requests below carry the same k,p. Each row is the state after the named event. Every durable state is Z or P_b, so I holds on every row.
Event | Q_R | V | Q_A | T | E/D
initial | - | - | - | - | Z
SEND a | a | - | - | - | Z
RECEIVE a | - | aR | - | - | Z
CRASH before PROCESS | - | - | - | a:L0 | Z
RESTART | - | - | - | a:L0 | Z
timeout | - | - | - | a:L0 | Z
agent restore | - | - | - | a:L0 | Z
SEND retry b | b | - | - | a:L0 | Z
RECEIVE b | - | bR | - | a:L0 | Z
PROCESS b | - | bC | - | a:L0 | P_b
ACK_ENQUEUE b | - | - | alpha_b | a:L0,b:F | P_b
ACK_DELIVER alpha_b | - | - | - | a:L0,b:F | P_b
J records alpha_b as delivered in the last row. Delivery a never reappears; only the new retry b creates the effect. Immediately before the crash, |Q_R|=0 but one unprocessed request still exists in V. Immediately afterward both queued and unprocessed-worker counts are zero. This resolves the earlier ambiguous q=0 notation.

reasoning_steps.title: T5 boundary control: crash after commit, before acknowledgment enqueue
reasoning_steps.argument:
This is the other crash boundary mentioned in the prior T5 description. I holds on every row, now using Z or P_a.
Event | Q_R | V | Q_A | T | E/D
initial | - | - | - | - | Z
SEND a | a | - | - | - | Z
RECEIVE a | - | aR | - | - | Z
PROCESS a | - | aC | - | - | P_a
CRASH before ACK_ENQUEUE | - | - | - | a:L1 | P_a
RESTART | - | - | - | a:L1 | P_a
timeout | - | - | - | a:L1 | P_a
agent restore | - | - | - | a:L1 | P_a
SEND retry b | b | - | - | a:L1 | P_a
RECEIVE b | - | bR | - | a:L1 | P_a
PROCESS b, replay | - | bC | - | a:L1 | P_a
ACK_ENQUEUE b | - | - | alpha_b | a:L1,b:F | P_a
ACK_DELIVER alpha_b | - | - | - | a:L1,b:F | P_a
No alpha_a was ever enqueued. The acknowledgment alpha_b contains the original r_a,id_a. J records alpha_b delivered. Actual completion survives a's lost reply; a's delivery itself is not reconstructed.

reasoning_steps.title: T8: a delayed request remains live through lookup and retry
reasoning_steps.argument:
Use the same event schedule for ordinary and atomic handlers. 'lookup' is a stipulated authoritative read of current effects, not a request added to this operation's Q; its query transport is outside this trace. It does not cancel or fence a. I_A holds on every row. I_O holds exactly on the Z rows and fails afterward by design.
Event | Q_R | V | Q_A | T | ordinary E/D | atomic E/D
initial | - | - | - | - | Z | Z
SEND a | a | - | - | - | Z | Z
DELAY a | a | - | - | - | Z | Z
timeout | a | - | - | - | Z | Z
lookup: no effect | a | - | - | - | Z | Z
SEND retry b | a,b | - | - | - | Z | Z
RECEIVE b | a | bR | - | - | Z | Z
PROCESS b | a | bC | - | - | O_b | P_b
ACK_ENQUEUE b | a | - | alpha_b | b:F | O_b | P_b
ACK_DELIVER alpha_b | a | - | - | b:F | O_b | P_b
release delay a | a | - | - | b:F | O_b | P_b
RECEIVE a | - | aR | - | b:F | O_b | P_b
PROCESS a | - | aC | - | b:F | O_ba | P_b
ACK_ENQUEUE a | - | - | alpha_a | a:F,b:F | O_ba | P_b
ACK_DELIVER alpha_a | - | - | - | a:F,b:F | O_ba | P_b
J records both acknowledgments delivered. Ordinary processing creates a second effect on PROCESS a. Atomic processing treats a as a replay and alpha_a returns r_b,id_b. The lookup was correct when made, yet left a live. Neither timeout nor delivery of alpha_b consumed a.

reasoning_steps.title: T12: a received and processed first
reasoning_steps.argument:
Two distinct deliveries have identical k,p. Both are dequeued before either PROCESS, allowing concurrent workers. Processing is serialized in order a,b. I holds on every row.
Event | Q_R | V | Q_A | T | E/D
initial | - | - | - | - | Z
SEND a | a | - | - | - | Z
SEND b | a,b | - | - | - | Z
RECEIVE a | b | aR | - | - | Z
RECEIVE b | - | aR,bR | - | - | Z
PROCESS a | - | aC,bR | - | - | P_a
PROCESS b, replay | - | aC,bC | - | - | P_a
ACK_ENQUEUE a | - | bC | alpha_a | a:F | P_a
ACK_ENQUEUE b | - | - | alpha_a,alpha_b | a:F,b:F | P_a
ACK_DELIVER alpha_a | - | - | alpha_b | a:F,b:F | P_a
ACK_DELIVER alpha_b | - | - | - | a:F,b:F | P_a
Both acknowledgments carry r_a,id_a; J records both delivered. Dequeuing b while D is absent does not reserve permission to create an effect: its PROCESS tests D after a's serialized commit.

reasoning_steps.title: T12: b received and processed first
reasoning_steps.argument:
Reverse delivery and processing order to b,a, retaining the same two sends. I holds on every row.
Event | Q_R | V | Q_A | T | E/D
initial | - | - | - | - | Z
SEND a | a | - | - | - | Z
SEND b | a,b | - | - | - | Z
RECEIVE b | a | bR | - | - | Z
RECEIVE a | - | aR,bR | - | - | Z
PROCESS b | - | aR,bC | - | - | P_b
PROCESS a, replay | - | aC,bC | - | - | P_b
ACK_ENQUEUE b | - | aC | alpha_b | b:F | P_b
ACK_ENQUEUE a | - | - | alpha_a,alpha_b | a:F,b:F | P_b
ACK_DELIVER alpha_b | - | - | alpha_a | a:F,b:F | P_b
ACK_DELIVER alpha_a | - | - | - | a:F,b:F | P_b
Both acknowledgments carry r_b,id_b; J records both delivered. Receive order need not equal processing order: after both RECEIVE events, the ready-worker state is identical in these tables. Choosing either PROCESS first therefore also covers the crossed receive/processing orders. The unique effect ID may differ across alternative executions; within each execution both replies identify its single effect.

assumptions: The modeled operation is ledger-backed, and all its effects occur through the defined PROCESS transition; E and D initially are empty.

RECEIVE is destructive dequeue into volatile execution state, with no retained broker lease or automatic redelivery. The independent envelope pool Q survives service crashes; explicit network drops remain possible.

Atomic mode serializes the current-D test, effect creation, and completed-record write in one crash-durable transition. Records are retained, operation keys do not collide, and all retries in these traces preserve the same full payload and key.

PROCESS and ACK_ENQUEUE are distinct abstract transitions; ACK_ENQUEUE atomically transfers a processed worker into one pending acknowledgment. Crashes preserve durable E/D and Q but erase all workers.
The manual traces use exactly the displayed schedules. They establish no fairness or eventual-processing property for arbitrary executions.

skeptic_output.solution_claim: Conditional on empty initial E/D, effects occurring only through the defined handler, destructive dequeue without automatic redelivery, crash-surviving Q, serialized crash-durable effect/record updates, retained records, noncolliding stable keys and payloads, and the displayed schedules, the request lifecycle is determinate and the atomic T5, T8, and T12 traces preserve E/D correspondence. skeptic_output.argument_summary: RECEIVE moves each fresh delivery ID from Q_R into a ready worker; PROCESS changes its phase and, in atomic mode, creates or reuses one matching effect-record pair; ACK_ENQUEUE moves the processed worker into a terminal request record and creates one acknowledgment. CRASH transfers all workers to terminal loss records while preserving durable state and queued envelopes. These transitions preserve the disjoint request-accounting partition. The manually checked traces instantiate this lifecycle consistently. reasoning_steps.title: State, identifiers, and table notation
reasoning_steps.argument: Retain S=(E,D,L,Q,V,J) from the supplied extract of artifact 4435b6ec-fefc-43a1-8706-a3a6794dbbe5. E is the durable effect multiset; D is the durable completed-record map; L is agent state; J is evaluator-only event history. Partition Q into request envelopes Q_R and acknowledgment envelopes Q_A. A request is (x,k,p), where delivery ID x is globally fresh, independently of stable operation key k. An acknowledgment has a fresh envelope ID alpha_x, correlation field x, and the processing outcome. Retries use a new delivery ID but the same k,p. Q is an independently maintained network-envelope pool: it survives service crashes but permits explicit DROP. It is not a durable broker with automatic redelivery. V contains a service up/down flag and volatile workers xR=(x,k,p,ready) or xC=(x,k,p,processed,outcome). Multiple workers are allowed. Tables display worker entries only; CRASH makes the service down and RESTART makes it up. '-' means empty. T is an evaluator-only terminal-request map derived from J, not additional recoverable service state: L0=lost before processing, L1=processed but reply lost before enqueue, F=handler finished with acknowledgment enqueued, X=explicitly dropped from Q_R. Each trace starts with empty E,D,Q,V,T and an up service.

review.rationale: As premises of the explicitly conditional claim, fresh delivery identifiers, stable operation identity, separate request/acknowledgment pools, and volatile worker phases give an unambiguous state representation. T is evaluator bookkeeping, not a hidden service recovery mechanism.

reasoning_steps.title: SEND, RECEIVE, delay, and drop
reasoning_steps.argument: SEND(x,k,p) adds exactly one fresh request envelope x to Q_R. RECEIVE(x) requires an up service and an eligible x in Q_R; it atomically removes x from Q_R and installs xR in V. RECEIVE changes neither E nor D and creates no acknowledgment. No copy or lease for x remains in Q. DELAY(x) makes no location change and merely withholds its RECEIVE until release. DROP(x) removes x from Q_R and records T[x]=X; dropping an acknowledgment instead removes its envelope from Q_A and records that acknowledgment's loss in J. A timeout does not remove an envelope or worker. Agent restore changes L only. There is no implicit duplicate delivery: an explicit retry is a new SEND with a fresh delivery ID.

review.rationale: The defined destructive RECEIVE leaves exactly one worker and no queued copy. DROP terminates a queued request, whereas delay and timeout preserve its location. These premises determine consumption without assuming broker redelivery.

reasoning_steps.title: PROCESS is separate from acknowledgment enqueue
reasoning_steps.argument: PROCESS(x) requires xR and an up service. In atomic mode, it tests current D at the serialized processing point, not at RECEIVE. If D[k] is absent, it atomically appends e=(effect_id,k,p) to E and installs D[k]=(p,result,effect_id). If D[k] matches p, it leaves E,D unchanged and obtains the recorded result and effect ID. If the payload differs, it leaves E,D unchanged and obtains a mismatch rejection. The transition replaces xR with xC carrying that outcome; x remains absent from Q_R. ACK_ENQUEUE(x) requires xC, inserts alpha_x into Q_A, removes xC from V, and records T[x]=F. This enqueue/removal is one abstract transition, so it cannot emit two acknowledgments for one worker. ACK_DELIVER(alpha_x) removes that envelope from Q_A, appends its correlated response to L, and records delivery in J. It does not change T[x], E, or D. For the ordinary control, PROCESS always appends a fresh effect and leaves D empty, then creates xC in the same way.

review.rationale: The current-D test at the serialized PROCESS point prevents an earlier RECEIVE from reserving an absent-key write. Atomic creation, read-only replay, and rejection are distinct from enqueue, which removes the worker and therefore cannot be repeated for it.

reasoning_steps.title: Crash boundary and request accounting
reasoning_steps.argument: CRASH clears every worker from V and sets the service down. For each xR it records T[x]=L0; for each xC it records T[x]=L1. It preserves E,D,Q_R,Q_A,L and prior terminal records. RESTART sets the service up with no workers; it reconstructs no consumed delivery. Thus a crash before RECEIVE leaves x queued, a crash after RECEIVE but before PROCESS loses x without an effect, a crash after PROCESS but before ACK_ENQUEUE loses only the volatile reply, and a crash after ACK_ENQUEUE leaves alpha_x pending in Q_A. A crash concurrent with atomic PROCESS is represented by either its before-state followed by CRASH or its complete after-state followed by CRASH; a partial E/D write is excluded by premise. The sent request IDs partition disjointly into Q_R, worker IDs in V, and terminal IDs in T. SEND introduces one ID, RECEIVE transfers it, PROCESS changes its worker phase, and enqueue/drop/crash transfers it to T. This proves complete request accounting inductively. Ack IDs similarly partition into Q_A and the delivered/dropped acknowledgment events in J. No automatic redelivery occurs after a pre-commit crash in this model; durable lease/redelivery semantics would be a different model.

review.rationale: Each transition either introduces one fresh sent ID or transfers an existing ID between disjoint request locations and terminal bookkeeping. Clearing workers on crash gives L0 or L1 according to phase and leaves queued requests and acknowledgments intact. The four crash-boundary outcomes follow from those rules.

reasoning_steps.title: Durable invariant and ledger abbreviations
reasoning_steps.argument: For each key, invariant I is: either D[k] is absent and E contains no effect for k, or D[k]=(p,r,id) and E contains exactly one effect for k, namely (id,k,p), whose recorded result is r. Define Z=(E=empty,D=empty). Define P_x=(E={e_x},D[k]=(p,r_x,id_x)), with e_x=(id_x,k,p) created by delivery x. Define O_b=(E={e_b},D=empty) and O_ba=(E={e_b,e_a},D=empty) for the ordinary control. Z and every P_x satisfy I, including full payload and identifier correspondence, not just counts. O_b and O_ba fail I because ordinary mode intentionally has no D record; O_b still has at-most-one effect, whereas O_ba does not. In atomic mode, first PROCESS creates one matching pair, replay/rejection preserve it, and every other lifecycle transition leaves E,D unchanged. This proves I from empty initialization despite crashes and concurrent workers. It supplies safety only: loss of every ready worker can leave Z forever.

review.rationale: From empty E/D, the absent-key branch creates exactly one matching pair, replay and rejection preserve it, and all transport transitions leave it unchanged. Serialization covers multiple ready workers. Ordinary-mode states correctly fail record correspondence without automatically failing at-most-one until a second effect occurs.

reasoning_steps.title: T5: consumed request lost immediately before commit
reasoning_steps.argument:
All requests below carry the same k,p. Each row is the state after the named event. Every durable state is Z or P_b, so I holds on every row.
Event | Q_R | V | Q_A | T | E/D
initial | - | - | - | - | Z
SEND a | a | - | - | - | Z
RECEIVE a | - | aR | - | - | Z
CRASH before PROCESS | - | - | - | a:L0 | Z
RESTART | - | - | - | a:L0 | Z
timeout | - | - | - | a:L0 | Z
agent restore | - | - | - | a:L0 | Z
SEND retry b | b | - | - | a:L0 | Z
RECEIVE b | - | bR | - | a:L0 | Z
PROCESS b | - | bC | - | a:L0 | P_b
ACK_ENQUEUE b | - | - | alpha_b | a:L0,b:F | P_b
ACK_DELIVER alpha_b | - | - | - | a:L0,b:F | P_b
J records alpha_b as delivered in the last row. Delivery a never reappears; only the new retry b creates the effect. Immediately before the crash, |Q_R|=0 but one unprocessed request still exists in V. Immediately afterward both queued and unprocessed-worker counts are zero. This resolves the earlier ambiguous q=0 notation.

review.rationale: The table transfers a from Q_R to aR, then to terminal L0 on crash, with E/D still empty. Only fresh retry b commits. Its acknowledgment is enqueued and delivered once; neither a nor its reply reappears. Every row satisfies request accounting and the atomic invariant.

reasoning_steps.title: T5 boundary control: crash after commit, before acknowledgment enqueue
reasoning_steps.argument:
This is the other crash boundary mentioned in the prior T5 description. I holds on every row, now using Z or P_a.
Event | Q_R | V | Q_A | T | E/D
initial | - | - | - | - | Z
SEND a | a | - | - | - | Z
RECEIVE a | - | aR | - | - | Z
PROCESS a | - | aC | - | - | P_a
CRASH before ACK_ENQUEUE | - | - | - | a:L1 | P_a
RESTART | - | - | - | a:L1 | P_a
timeout | - | - | - | a:L1 | P_a
agent restore | - | - | - | a:L1 | P_a
SEND retry b | b | - | - | a:L1 | P_a
RECEIVE b | - | bR | - | a:L1 | P_a
PROCESS b, replay | - | bC | - | a:L1 | P_a
ACK_ENQUEUE b | - | - | alpha_b | a:L1,b:F | P_a
ACK_DELIVER alpha_b | - | - | - | a:L1,b:F | P_a
No alpha_a was ever enqueued. The acknowledgment alpha_b contains the original r_a,id_a. J records alpha_b delivered. Actual completion survives a's lost reply; a's delivery itself is not reconstructed.

review.rationale: PROCESS a installs P_a before the crash. The crash removes aC without creating alpha_a, and replay by b preserves P_a and returns its original result and identifier. All pending and terminal IDs remain accounted for.

reasoning_steps.title: T8: a delayed request remains live through lookup and retry
reasoning_steps.argument:
Use the same event schedule for ordinary and atomic handlers. 'lookup' is a stipulated authoritative read of current effects, not a request added to this operation's Q; its query transport is outside this trace. It does not cancel or fence a. I_A holds on every row. I_O holds exactly on the Z rows and fails afterward by design.
Event | Q_R | V | Q_A | T | ordinary E/D | atomic E/D
initial | - | - | - | - | Z | Z
SEND a | a | - | - | - | Z | Z
DELAY a | a | - | - | - | Z | Z
timeout | a | - | - | - | Z | Z
lookup: no effect | a | - | - | - | Z | Z
SEND retry b | a,b | - | - | - | Z | Z
RECEIVE b | a | bR | - | - | Z | Z
PROCESS b | a | bC | - | - | O_b | P_b
ACK_ENQUEUE b | a | - | alpha_b | b:F | O_b | P_b
ACK_DELIVER alpha_b | a | - | - | b:F | O_b | P_b
release delay a | a | - | - | b:F | O_b | P_b
RECEIVE a | - | aR | - | b:F | O_b | P_b
PROCESS a | - | aC | - | b:F | O_ba | P_b
ACK_ENQUEUE a | - | - | alpha_a | a:F,b:F | O_ba | P_b
ACK_DELIVER alpha_a | - | - | - | a:F,b:F | O_ba | P_b
J records both acknowledgments delivered. Ordinary processing creates a second effect on PROCESS a. Atomic processing treats a as a replay and alpha_a returns r_b,id_b. The lookup was correct when made, yet left a live. Neither timeout nor delivery of alpha_b consumed a.

review.rationale: The stipulated instantaneous lookup reads empty effects while a remains queued. Processing b does not consume a. Later processing a creates a second ordinary effect or replays the atomic record. Both acknowledgments and terminal request records follow the stated transitions. This tests unfenced lookup only, not stronger lookup protocols.

reasoning_steps.title: T12: a received and processed first
reasoning_steps.argument:
Two distinct deliveries have identical k,p. Both are dequeued before either PROCESS, allowing concurrent workers. Processing is serialized in order a,b. I holds on every row.
Event | Q_R | V | Q_A | T | E/D
initial | - | - | - | - | Z
SEND a | a | - | - | - | Z
SEND b | a,b | - | - | - | Z
RECEIVE a | b | aR | - | - | Z
RECEIVE b | - | aR,bR | - | - | Z
PROCESS a | - | aC,bR | - | - | P_a
PROCESS b, replay | - | aC,bC | - | - | P_a
ACK_ENQUEUE a | - | bC | alpha_a | a:F | P_a
ACK_ENQUEUE b | - | - | alpha_a,alpha_b | a:F,b:F | P_a
ACK_DELIVER alpha_a | - | - | alpha_b | a:F,b:F | P_a
ACK_DELIVER alpha_b | - | - | - | a:F,b:F | P_a
Both acknowledgments carry r_a,id_a; J records both delivered. Dequeuing b while D is absent does not reserve permission to create an effect: its PROCESS tests D after a's serialized commit.

review.rationale: Both deliveries are ready before processing. PROCESS a creates P_a; PROCESS b reads the resulting D and replays it. The subsequent enqueue and delivery rows conserve both request and acknowledgment IDs and return the same effect identifier.

reasoning_steps.title: T12: b received and processed first
reasoning_steps.argument:
Reverse delivery and processing order to b,a, retaining the same two sends. I holds on every row.
Event | Q_R | V | Q_A | T | E/D
initial | - | - | - | - | Z
SEND a | a | - | - | - | Z
SEND b | a,b | - | - | - | Z
RECEIVE b | a | bR | - | - | Z
RECEIVE a | - | aR,bR | - | - | Z
PROCESS b | - | aR,bC | - | - | P_b
PROCESS a, replay | - | aC,bC | - | - | P_b
ACK_ENQUEUE b | - | aC | alpha_b | b:F | P_b
ACK_ENQUEUE a | - | - | alpha_a,alpha_b | a:F,b:F | P_b
ACK_DELIVER alpha_b | - | - | alpha_a | a:F,b:F | P_b
ACK_DELIVER alpha_a | - | - | - | a:F,b:F | P_b
Both acknowledgments carry r_b,id_b; J records both delivered. Receive order need not equal processing order: after both RECEIVE events, the ready-worker state is identical in these tables. Choosing either PROCESS first therefore also covers the crossed receive/processing orders. The unique effect ID may differ across alternative executions; within each execution both replies identify its single effect.

review.rationale: Reversing the first PROCESS creates P_b and makes a a replay. Once both RECEIVE events have occurred, the ready-worker state is the same regardless of receive order, so either first PROCESS also covers the crossed orders. Identifiers need agree within, not across, alternative executions.

objective_review.argument_summary: RECEIVE moves each fresh delivery ID from Q_R into a ready worker; PROCESS changes its phase and, in atomic mode, creates or reuses one matching effect-record pair; ACK_ENQUEUE moves the processed worker into a terminal request record and creates one acknowledgment. CRASH transfers all workers to terminal loss records while preserving durable state and queued envelopes. These transitions preserve the disjoint request-accounting partition. The manually checked traces instantiate this lifecycle consistently. T8 creates two ordinary effects but only one atomic effect; both T12 processing orders create one pair and return its identifier to both deliveries. argument_steps.title: State, identifiers, and table notation
argument_steps.argument: Retain S=(E,D,L,Q,V,J) from the supplied extract of artifact 4435b6ec-fefc-43a1-8706-a3a6794dbbe5. E is the durable effect multiset; D is the durable completed-record map; L is agent state; J is evaluator-only event history. Partition Q into request envelopes Q_R and acknowledgment envelopes Q_A. A request is (x,k,p), where delivery ID x is globally fresh, independently of stable operation key k. An acknowledgment has a fresh envelope ID alpha_x, correlation field x, and the processing outcome. Retries use a new delivery ID but the same k,p. Q is an independently maintained network-envelope pool: it survives service crashes but permits explicit DROP. It is not a durable broker with automatic redelivery. V contains a service up/down flag and volatile workers xR=(x,k,p,ready) or xC=(x,k,p,processed,outcome). Multiple workers are allowed. Tables display worker entries only; CRASH makes the service down and RESTART makes it up. '-' means empty. T is an evaluator-only terminal-request map derived from J, not additional recoverable service state: L0=lost before processing, L1=processed but reply lost before enqueue, F=handler finished with acknowledgment enqueued, X=explicitly dropped from Q_R. Each trace starts with empty E,D,Q,V,T and an up service.

review.rationale: As premises of the explicitly conditional claim, fresh delivery identifiers, stable operation identity, separate request/acknowledgment pools, and volatile worker phases give an unambiguous state representation. T is evaluator bookkeeping, not a hidden service recovery mechanism.

argument_steps.title: SEND, RECEIVE, delay, and drop
argument_steps.argument: SEND(x,k,p) adds exactly one fresh request envelope x to Q_R. RECEIVE(x) requires an up service and an eligible x in Q_R; it atomically removes x from Q_R and installs xR in V. RECEIVE changes neither E nor D and creates no acknowledgment. No copy or lease for x remains in Q. DELAY(x) makes no location change and merely withholds its RECEIVE until release. DROP(x) removes x from Q_R and records T[x]=X; dropping an acknowledgment instead removes its envelope from Q_A and records that acknowledgment's loss in J. A timeout does not remove an envelope or worker. Agent restore changes L only. There is no implicit duplicate delivery: an explicit retry is a new SEND with a fresh delivery ID.

review.rationale: The defined destructive RECEIVE leaves exactly one worker and no queued copy. DROP terminates a queued request, whereas delay and timeout preserve its location. These premises determine consumption without assuming broker redelivery.

argument_steps.title: PROCESS is separate from acknowledgment enqueue
argument_steps.argument: PROCESS(x) requires xR and an up service. In atomic mode, it tests current D at the serialized processing point, not at RECEIVE. If D[k] is absent, it atomically appends e=(effect_id,k,p) to E and installs D[k]=(p,result,effect_id). If D[k] matches p, it leaves E,D unchanged and obtains the recorded result and effect ID. If the payload differs, it leaves E,D unchanged and obtains a mismatch rejection. The transition replaces xR with xC carrying that outcome; x remains absent from Q_R. ACK_ENQUEUE(x) requires xC, inserts alpha_x into Q_A, removes xC from V, and records T[x]=F. This enqueue/removal is one abstract transition, so it cannot emit two acknowledgments for one worker. ACK_DELIVER(alpha_x) removes that envelope from Q_A, appends its correlated response to L, and records delivery in J. It does not change T[x], E, or D. For the ordinary control, PROCESS always appends a fresh effect and leaves D empty, then creates xC in the same way.

review.rationale: The current-D test at the serialized PROCESS point prevents an earlier RECEIVE from reserving an absent-key write. Atomic creation, read-only replay, and rejection are distinct from enqueue, which removes the worker and therefore cannot be repeated for it.

argument_steps.title: Crash boundary and request accounting
argument_steps.argument: CRASH clears every worker from V and sets the service down. For each xR it records T[x]=L0; for each xC it records T[x]=L1. It preserves E,D,Q_R,Q_A,L and prior terminal records. RESTART sets the service up with no workers; it reconstructs no consumed delivery. Thus a crash before RECEIVE leaves x queued, a crash after RECEIVE but before PROCESS loses x without an effect, a crash after PROCESS but before ACK_ENQUEUE loses only the volatile reply, and a crash after ACK_ENQUEUE leaves alpha_x pending in Q_A. A crash concurrent with atomic PROCESS is represented by either its before-state followed by CRASH or its complete after-state followed by CRASH; a partial E/D write is excluded by premise. The sent request IDs partition disjointly into Q_R, worker IDs in V, and terminal IDs in T. SEND introduces one ID, RECEIVE transfers it, PROCESS changes its worker phase, and enqueue/drop/crash transfers it to T. This proves complete request accounting inductively. Ack IDs similarly partition into Q_A and the delivered/dropped acknowledgment events in J. No automatic redelivery occurs after a pre-commit crash in this model; durable lease/redelivery semantics would be a different model.

review.rationale: Each transition either introduces one fresh sent ID or transfers an existing ID between disjoint request locations and terminal bookkeeping. Clearing workers on crash gives L0 or L1 according to phase and leaves queued requests and acknowledgments intact. The four crash-boundary outcomes follow from those rules.

argument_steps.title: Durable invariant and ledger abbreviations
argument_steps.argument: For each key, invariant I is: either D[k] is absent and E contains no effect for k, or D[k]=(p,r,id) and E contains exactly one effect for k, namely (id,k,p), whose recorded result is r. Define Z=(E=empty,D=empty). Define P_x=(E={e_x},D[k]=(p,r_x,id_x)), with e_x=(id_x,k,p) created by delivery x. Define O_b=(E={e_b},D=empty) and O_ba=(E={e_b,e_a},D=empty) for the ordinary control. Z and every P_x satisfy I, including full payload and identifier correspondence, not just counts. O_b and O_ba fail I because ordinary mode intentionally has no D record; O_b still has at-most-one effect, whereas O_ba does not. In atomic mode, first PROCESS creates one matching pair, replay/rejection preserve it, and every other lifecycle transition leaves E,D unchanged. This proves I from empty initialization despite crashes and concurrent workers. It supplies safety only: loss of every ready worker can leave Z forever.

review.rationale: From empty E/D, the absent-key branch creates exactly one matching pair, replay and rejection preserve it, and all transport transitions leave it unchanged. Serialization covers multiple ready workers. Ordinary-mode states correctly fail record correspondence without automatically failing at-most-one until a second effect occurs.

argument_steps.title: T5: consumed request lost immediately before commit
argument_steps.argument:
All requests below carry the same k,p. Each row is the state after the named event. Every durable state is Z or P_b, so I holds on every row.
Event | Q_R | V | Q_A | T | E/D
initial | - | - | - | - | Z
SEND a | a | - | - | - | Z
RECEIVE a | - | aR | - | - | Z
CRASH before PROCESS | - | - | - | a:L0 | Z
RESTART | - | - | - | a:L0 | Z
timeout | - | - | - | a:L0 | Z
agent restore | - | - | - | a:L0 | Z
SEND retry b | b | - | - | a:L0 | Z
RECEIVE b | - | bR | - | a:L0 | Z
PROCESS b | - | bC | - | a:L0 | P_b
ACK_ENQUEUE b | - | - | alpha_b | a:L0,b:F | P_b
ACK_DELIVER alpha_b | - | - | - | a:L0,b:F | P_b
J records alpha_b as delivered in the last row. Delivery a never reappears; only the new retry b creates the effect. Immediately before the crash, |Q_R|=0 but one unprocessed request still exists in V. Immediately afterward both queued and unprocessed-worker counts are zero. This resolves the earlier ambiguous q=0 notation.

review.rationale: The table transfers a from Q_R to aR, then to terminal L0 on crash, with E/D still empty. Only fresh retry b commits. Its acknowledgment is enqueued and delivered once; neither a nor its reply reappears. Every row satisfies request accounting and the atomic invariant.

argument_steps.title: T5 boundary control: crash after commit, before acknowledgment enqueue
argument_steps.argument:
This is the other crash boundary mentioned in the prior T5 description. I holds on every row, now using Z or P_a.
Event | Q_R | V | Q_A | T | E/D
initial | - | - | - | - | Z
SEND a | a | - | - | - | Z
RECEIVE a | - | aR | - | - | Z
PROCESS a | - | aC | - | - | P_a
CRASH before ACK_ENQUEUE | - | - | - | a:L1 | P_a
RESTART | - | - | - | a:L1 | P_a
timeout | - | - | - | a:L1 | P_a
agent restore | - | - | - | a:L1 | P_a
SEND retry b | b | - | - | a:L1 | P_a
RECEIVE b | - | bR | - | a:L1 | P_a
PROCESS b, replay | - | bC | - | a:L1 | P_a
ACK_ENQUEUE b | - | - | alpha_b | a:L1,b:F | P_a
ACK_DELIVER alpha_b | - | - | - | a:L1,b:F | P_a
No alpha_a was ever enqueued. The acknowledgment alpha_b contains the original r_a,id_a. J records alpha_b delivered. Actual completion survives a's lost reply; a's delivery itself is not reconstructed.

review.rationale: PROCESS a installs P_a before the crash. The crash removes aC without creating alpha_a, and replay by b preserves P_a and returns its original result and identifier. All pending and terminal IDs remain accounted for.

argument_steps.title: T8: a delayed request remains live through lookup and retry
argument_steps.argument:
Use the same event schedule for ordinary and atomic handlers. 'lookup' is a stipulated authoritative read of current effects, not a request added to this operation's Q; its query transport is outside this trace. It does not cancel or fence a. I_A holds on every row. I_O holds exactly on the Z rows and fails afterward by design.
Event | Q_R | V | Q_A | T | ordinary E/D | atomic E/D
initial | - | - | - | - | Z | Z
SEND a | a | - | - | - | Z | Z
DELAY a | a | - | - | - | Z | Z
timeout | a | - | - | - | Z | Z
lookup: no effect | a | - | - | - | Z | Z
SEND retry b | a,b | - | - | - | Z | Z
RECEIVE b | a | bR | - | - | Z | Z
PROCESS b | a | bC | - | - | O_b | P_b
ACK_ENQUEUE b | a | - | alpha_b | b:F | O_b | P_b
ACK_DELIVER alpha_b | a | - | - | b:F | O_b | P_b
release delay a | a | - | - | b:F | O_b | P_b
RECEIVE a | - | aR | - | b:F | O_b | P_b
PROCESS a | - | aC | - | b:F | O_ba | P_b
ACK_ENQUEUE a | - | - | alpha_a | a:F,b:F | O_ba | P_b
ACK_DELIVER alpha_a | - | - | - | a:F,b:F | O_ba | P_b
J records both acknowledgments delivered. Ordinary processing creates a second effect on PROCESS a. Atomic processing treats a as a replay and alpha_a returns r_b,id_b. The lookup was correct when made, yet left a live. Neither timeout nor delivery of alpha_b consumed a.

review.rationale: The stipulated instantaneous lookup reads empty effects while a remains queued. Processing b does not consume a. Later processing a creates a second ordinary effect or replays the atomic record. Both acknowledgments and terminal request records follow the stated transitions. This tests unfenced lookup only, not stronger lookup protocols.

argument_steps.title: T12: a received and processed first
argument_steps.argument:
Two distinct deliveries have identical k,p. Both are dequeued before either PROCESS, allowing concurrent workers. Processing is serialized in order a,b. I holds on every row.
Event | Q_R | V | Q_A | T | E/D
initial | - | - | - | - | Z
SEND a | a | - | - | - | Z
SEND b | a,b | - | - | - | Z
RECEIVE a | b | aR | - | - | Z
RECEIVE b | - | aR,bR | - | - | Z
PROCESS a | - | aC,bR | - | - | P_a
PROCESS b, replay | - | aC,bC | - | - | P_a
ACK_ENQUEUE a | - | bC | alpha_a | a:F | P_a
ACK_ENQUEUE b | - | - | alpha_a,alpha_b | a:F,b:F | P_a
ACK_DELIVER alpha_a | - | - | alpha_b | a:F,b:F | P_a
ACK_DELIVER alpha_b | - | - | - | a:F,b:F | P_a
Both acknowledgments carry r_a,id_a; J records both delivered. Dequeuing b while D is absent does not reserve permission to create an effect: its PROCESS tests D after a's serialized commit.

review.rationale: Both deliveries are ready before processing. PROCESS a creates P_a; PROCESS b reads the resulting D and replays it. The subsequent enqueue and delivery rows conserve both request and acknowledgment IDs and return the same effect identifier.

argument_steps.title: T12: b received and processed first
argument_steps.argument:
Reverse delivery and processing order to b,a, retaining the same two sends. I holds on every row.
Event | Q_R | V | Q_A | T | E/D
initial | - | - | - | - | Z
SEND a | a | - | - | - | Z
SEND b | a,b | - | - | - | Z
RECEIVE b | a | bR | - | - | Z
RECEIVE a | - | aR,bR | - | - | Z
PROCESS b | - | aR,bC | - | - | P_b
PROCESS a, replay | - | aC,bC | - | - | P_b
ACK_ENQUEUE b | - | aC | alpha_b | b:F | P_b
ACK_ENQUEUE a | - | - | alpha_a,alpha_b | a:F,b:F | P_b
ACK_DELIVER alpha_b | - | - | alpha_a | a:F,b:F | P_b
ACK_DELIVER alpha_a | - | - | - | a:F,b:F | P_b
Both acknowledgments carry r_b,id_b; J records both delivered. Receive order need not equal processing order: after both RECEIVE events, the ready-worker state is identical in these tables. Choosing either PROCESS first therefore also covers the crossed receive/processing orders. The unique effect ID may differ across alternative executions; within each execution both replies identify its single effect.

review.rationale: Reversing the first PROCESS creates P_b and makes a a replay. Once both RECEIVE events have occurred, the ready-worker state is the same regardless of receive order, so either first PROCESS also covers the crossed orders. Identifiers need agree within, not across, alternative executions.
